(p-376) Sūrat al-Zukhruf

Its purpose is good news of the elevation of this Ummah through intellect and wisdom, so that they become the highest of the nations in knowledge and in what arises from it in terms of status. Their guidance by a command from before Him (*ladunnī*), which is among the most wondrous of wonders and belongs to the elite, is in the second degree of strangeness. And that is a matter they must have, even if their aversion to it is intense and they turn away from it. It is indeed a reminder for you and your people, so that you may become worthy of Paradise, in which is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in, and in which you will abide. He did not say "and they," and the naming of this surah "al-Zukhruf" (ornaments) indicates this, because in its verse [it is stated] that if He had willed that disbelief should encompass all people, He would have encompassed them with abundant blessings. But He did not encompass them thereby. Rather, He differentiated among them: He made some of them poor and increased their misery and harm, and divided their affairs, so that it would be easy to turn them back from disbelief, to which their natures, their desires, and their deficiencies had led them, by what they witness of the ugliness of injustice and aggression, toward what they see of the beauties of the religion and faith, and the sweetness of submission to the Sovereign, the Judge. Thus kings and notables will submit to them, and the criterion (*furqān*) will be theirs over all the people of disobedience.

*In the name of Allah* (Bismillāh), the One to whom belong the keys (*maqālīd*) of all affairs, so He (p-377) elevates whom He wills, even if his lowliness is prolonged. *The Most Gracious* (al-Raḥmān), whose benevolence all His creation has attained according to their ranks with Him. *The Most Merciful* (al-Raḥīm), who accepts whom He wills, bringing him to that which draws him near to Him in nearness, even if he has reached the furthest limit of distance.

* *

﴿Ḥā' Mīm﴾: the wisdom of Muhammad, which Allah revealed to him.

Since [the previous surah] concluded with [a statement about] what He made what was revealed to him (ṣallā Allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam) a light by which He guides whom He wills, and since it had been established in the previous surah what he has of majesty, namely that it is His revelation, and it concluded that there is no command that goes out from Him (glorified is He), this indicates that He will turn them back from their error, and they were scheming to return. The situation therefore required the utmost emphasis. And since Allah the Exalted's swearing by things is an announcement of the majesty of the wisdom contained in them and an alert to contemplation of the secrets He deposited in them, which qualified them to be sworn by, He opened this surah by glorifying this revelation by swearing by it, as an urging to reflect upon the aspects that made it fit to be an oath, and then [to glorify] its effect.

He said: ﴿By the Book﴾ (p-378), that is, and the inimitability (*iʿjāz*) of this [Book] that gathers every good and other kinds of its greatness, ﴿the Clear﴾, that is, clear in itself, and making clear all that is in it of greatness, legislation, customs (*sunan*), subtle meanings, knowledge, and favors, with a great and healing clarification.

He said: ﴿By the Book﴾ (p-378), that is, and the inimitability (*iʿjāz*) of this [Book] that gathers every good and other kinds of its greatness, ﴿the Clear﴾, that is, clear in itself, and making clear all that is in it of greatness, legislation, customs (*sunan*), subtle meanings, knowledge, and favors, with a great and healing clarification.

When they denied that he could bring them back from what they were in and that it could come from Allah, he stressed what refutes them in His saying earlier, at the end of Surah al-Shura, that it is "a light, a guidance, and a spirit," expressing this with *ja'l* (making, appointing) rather than *inzal* (sending down), because all the preceding surahs indicated this, sometimes explicitly and sometimes with the word *wahy* (revelation). So He said, swearing by the Book to show the greatness of the Book. Al-Samin said: "Among the eloquence (*balaghah*) recognized by them is that the oath and what is sworn to belong to the same category. This holds if by 'the Book' is meant the Qur'an. If it is meant more generally, then the oath is by part of it." He turned the speech to the locus of greatness, honouring the Book: ﴿Indeed, We have made it﴾, that is, We made it, placed it, and named it, in correspondence with its state, by expressing its meanings through what belongs to Our greatness. ﴿A Qur'an﴾, that is, while being a collection of letters and meanings, and while being comprehensive and distinguishing between (p-379) the ambiguous matters. ﴿In Arabic﴾, that is, operating according to the rules of their tongue in literal and figurative usage, and figurative usage (*majaz*) is predominant in it, because it is more eloquent, especially metonymies (*kinayat*) and similes/allegories (*tamthilat*). He turned the speech away from addressing His Prophet ﷺ specifically to addressing them, honouring him ﷺ and them in what He intends for them, and alerting to the baseness of their condition at the time of its descent. So He said: ﴿so that you may understand﴾, that is, so that you, O Arabs, may be in hope, according to one whose hope is valid, that you will understand that it is from Us, and not contend against Us concerning it, and comprehend its meanings and all that is within human capacity of what is intended by its judgments and rulings, its wondrous description, its inimitable description and its order. Then you would abandon all that you are engaged in of contention. This act must occur, for when the All-Powerful expresses it with the particle of hope, He makes certain what its hope concerns, so that there is a difference between His speech and the speech of one who is incapable. This comprehensive Book will reach your farthest as it was presented to your nearest, and each of you knows that he is incapable of contending with a single verse of it in the beauty of its meaning, the soundness of its wording and the grandeur of its composition. Each word of it is arranged in the place where it cannot be shifted by advancing or delaying, nor can any part of it be replaced by something that conveys its meaning or stands in its place. This is most evident in the comparison of ﴿In retaliation there is life﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:179] with "Killing is more effective in preventing killing," and that is only part of a verse, so how about a verse or more? (p-380) Then the tyrants of your minds will submit to it, and the foreheads of your intellects will prostrate to it, and the lofty peaks of your thoughts will be humbled before its might. You will hasten to accept it, rush to memorize and bear it, knowing that it is a glory for you to which no glory comes close, and a might that no might approaches. Then whoever among you opposes it, far or near, child or parent, will reflect until all creation submits to it and the towering mountains become small before its greatness. The verse alludes to the verse in Fussilat:

﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said﴾ [Fussilat 41:44], and so on.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 4:

When they denied His exaltation out of obstinacy, though at times they acknowledged it, He said, emphasizing this and drawing attention to the fact that it (the Qur'an) is worthy of being sworn by, and increasing its exaltation, because there is no speech resembling it, nor does anything come near it in any way: ﴿And indeed it﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, and He placed the two adverbial phrases before the predicate, which is linked with the lam (of emphasis), to give them prominence, so as to convey at the very outset that its loftiness and wisdom are established in the Mother (of the Book), and that the Mother is in the utmost strangeness in His sight. ﴿In the Mother of the Book﴾, i.e., existing in the origin of every heavenly Book, which is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). He increased its honour by expressing it with "Our" (bladi, "with Us"), which is for the most special of the special, and the Majestic plural (nun al-'azamah). And He said (p-381), placing the adverbial phrase before the prepositional phrase, to convey that the Mother of the Book is among the most wondrous of the wondrous things with Him: ﴿with Us﴾, according to what it is there, ﴿is indeed Exalted﴾.

Since the exalted may be lofty without wisdom accompanying that loftiness, so that his loftiness is not firmly established, his structure collapses and his lowliness and nearness are diminished, He said: ﴿Wise﴾, i.e., eloquent in each of these two attributes, firmly rooted in them with a firmness that no book comes near, so that it is not opposed in the exaltedness of its wording, nor is it matched in the wisdom of its meaning; it is exalted and nothing is exalted above it by abrogation or otherwise. Rather, there it is written in letters and expressions surpassing and delightful, which rise above the understanding of the most intelligent of the wise, and it is impossible in any way for the most noble of the noble to attain them, except through the enlightenment of the Exalted, the Great, who is over all things Powerful.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When He, glory be to Him, deferred, through a test, the successors of the Children of Israel in their doubt regarding their Book, by His saying: ﴿And indeed those who were given the Book after them are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾ [al-Shura: 14], and enjoined upon His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to disassociate himself from their evil condition and to keep clear of their bad conduct, saying: ﴿And do not follow their desires, and say, "I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down"﴾ [al-Shura: 15], the praise of the Arabic Book was repeated, as in His saying: ﴿And thus We revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Shura: 7], and His saying: ﴿Allah is He who sent down the Book with truth and the balance﴾ [al-Shura: 17], and His saying: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ [al-Shura: 52] — to the end of the surah. He followed this with swearing by it and strengthened the praise of it, saying: ﴿Ha Mim﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 1], ﴿By the Clear Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 2], ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you might understand﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3], ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise﴾. When He made clear the great state of the Book and the magnificence of His blessing through it, He followed that by mentioning the abundance of His forgiveness and the beauty of His kindness to His servants and His mercy to them through His Book, despite their excess and the ugliness of their transgressions, saying: ﴿Shall We then withhold the reminder from you, turning away, because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 5]. And since in al-Shura He had mentioned His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He creates what He wills; He bestows female offspring on whom He wills and bestows males on whom He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 49], ﴿Or He gives them both males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ [al-Shura: 50], He made known that this occurs only by His power and will, and the course of action in this is to submit to what occurs, to be content with what He has apportioned and chosen. In this surah the Exalted rebuked those who transgressed and deviated, saying: ﴿And when one of them is given good news of what he attributes to the Most Merciful, his face becomes dark, and he suppresses his grief﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 17]. So here He completed the occurrence with what is connected to it. Likewise His saying: ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 27], and His saying in al-Zukhruf: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 33], to the end of it. — End.

(p. 383) When the repetition of this emphasis made clear that they were disparaging its loftiness and finding fault with its wondrous beauty, He did what they hate and refuse, in order to establish them in what Allah does not love or approve. He said, rebuking them: ﴿Shall We then turn away from you this Reminder...﴾, that is, shall We leave you alone and so turn aside and withdraw, ﴿from you﴾ specifically, from among the children of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, ﴿the Reminder﴾, that is, the admonition that brings honor, ﴿utterly﴾, that is, in such a way that Our state toward you is that of one who turns away and withdraws with the side of his neck, so We send you no Messenger and send down no Book with him. It is then a verbal object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: We strike [the Reminder away] because of Our turning away from you. Or it may be an adverbial expression (zarf) in the sense of "to one side," meaning: We strike it away from you to one side.

The compiler of al-'Ubab and al-Muhkam said: "I ḍaraba 'an al-shay'" means I withheld and turned away from it, and "ḍaraba 'anhu al-dhikr" and "aḍraba 'anhu" mean he diverted it. Imam 'Abd al-Haqq said in al-Wa'i: "The original sense of ḍaraba 'anhu al-dhikr is that when a rider mounts his beast and wishes to turn it from its course, he strikes it with his staff so that it swerves from its course toward the direction he wants. So the act of striking was placed in the position of diverting and turning aside." Al-Harawi said: al-Azhari said: "It is said: ḍarabtu 'anhu and aḍrabtu 'anhu with one meaning." Al-Nawawi quoted from him that he said: "The unaugmented form is rare."

The sum is that ḍarb (striking) is the bringing of one thing down upon another with force. Its unaugmented form is transitive to one object. If it is extended to another object by "'an," it carries the sense of diverting. When the hamza of causation (hamzat al-naql) is added, so that one says aḍrabtu 'anhu, the hamza makes the verb's effect restricted and conveys the removal of the striking. So the meaning of the verse is: "Shall We then strike away from you the Reminder, diverting it utterly," that is, turning away with intense aversion, as if We had struck the Reminder so that it would turn away from you, showing aversion like one who turns his back and presents the side of his neck.

Then He gave as the reason for their desire for this aversion, a reason that calls for approach, either punishment or repentance, saying: ﴿because﴾, that is, shall We do this because ﴿you were a people who exceed their bounds﴾, that is, because excess was your innate disposition and firmly rooted nature, and you were able to act on it through denying the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mocking what he brought, and ridiculing his affair. You are left alone either out of fear of your severity or in hope that you would be reminded without your repentance being sought. Here He made the cause (muqtada) an obstacle, for the one who exceeds bounds is most deserving of being reminded and most in need of admonition. This applies if he is near. As for the distant one, he is not paid attention to from the outset. Indeed, if he wished to drive him away...

According to the reading of Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i with the kasra on "inna" (if) as a conditional particle, the speech is framed in the most equitable manner, and the meaning is: "Shall We leave you uncared for and withhold the Reminder from you, while you are a people who may possibly be characterized by excess?" That is, the one who exceeds bounds is fit to be admonished and addressed with what turns him back from excess. You, although you claim to be reformers, cannot ward off from yourselves the possibility of excess. How then would the admonishing Reminder be averted from you, when you are in a state in which you could become excessive and thus need it? This is something no wise one would do with his servants. Rather, He, glory be to Him, out of His kindness and abundant goodness, does not abandon calling His servants to His mercy, even if they are excessive and have gone far in deviance, denial and obstinacy. So He calls them with the most eloquent proof, namely this Qur'an, which is the noblest of Books, upon the tongue of this Prophet, who is the greatest of the Messengers, so that whoever has been destined for guidance may be guided, and the proof may be established against others.

Since the meaning was that We would not leave you purposeless, it was as if it were said: "Far be it from you; We will surely raise you up just as We raised the Children of Israel, the descendants of Isaac, and Jesus, upon them be peace. Indeed, We sent to you, although you are the most exalted of people, a Messenger who is the noblest of you in lineage, the purest of you in soul, the loftiest of you in aspiration, the most judicious of you in intellect, the most faithful of you in trust, the most generous of you in character, and the most honoured of you among his kinsfolk." He joined this saying to give the Prophet (ﷺ) companionship, consolation, solace and comfort, with ﴿And how many a prophet We sent﴾, meaning: according to what We possess of power to do so and of the dazzling majesty that necessitates it.

Since sending takes various forms, He specified it by saying: ﴿among the prophets of the former peoples﴾.

Then he recounts their past condition, indicating that the state of creation continued in this manner. He says: ﴿And not﴾, that is, while the situation is that there does not ﴿come to them﴾, and he emphasized the universality by his saying: ﴿any prophet﴾, that is, to a nation after nation, and age after age, ﴿except that they were﴾, that is, by creation, nature and disposition, ﴿mocking him﴾, just as your people mocked. The placing of the adverbial phrase "bihi" (at him) before the verb indicates that their mockery of him was so intense in its exaggeration that it seems restricted to him.

(p-387)

When mockery of the king's messenger is mockery of the king himself, and kingdoms are sustained through governance that combines desire and fear and the instilling of awe, so that majesty is completed and greatness is established, then no sound mind could accept that a king would allow mockery of himself. Therefore, the destruction is made a consequence of mocking the messengers. He said: ﴿So We destroyed﴾. The original form would have been the pronoun (al-idmar, the use of a pronoun), but he used the explicit noun to clarify, since the ones of old were of such magnitude that it turned the style of address away from the pronoun toward the third person, turning toward His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as consolation for him and as a thorough warning to them. He said: ﴿stronger than them﴾, that is, than the Quraysh who mock you, ﴿in might﴾, in terms of number, multitude, strength and vigour. So what do they think of themselves, when they are weaker than those, if they persist in mocking the Messenger of Allah, the Most High?

When He mentioned the destruction of those people, He mentioned that their condition, in regard to destruction, was the weakest of conditions, so that these people might take heed. He said: ﴿and the example of the former peoples has passed﴾, that is, their destruction took place, and it became an example by which people are made to think of them from afar. He also mentioned in the Qur'an the report about him in a way that is fitting for one who points out an example. Rather, He mentioned that those whom the former peoples worshipped and relied upon were like the spider's house. So how about the former peoples themselves, and how about these? For the situation has led to their being weaker than the weakest of the spider's house. So let them await that there befall them the like of what befell those, at the hands of the soldiers of Allah, whether of mankind or of the angels.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 9:

Since the sense is: "If you asked them about those among the earlier peoples whom We have mentioned, of whose report they have heard, they would acknowledge what they have heard of their story, because We have not given them, in that matter, the boldness of brazen denial, given the natural disposition by which We have made them, in most of their conditions, truthful," the statement that follows it (p-388) is joined to it by conjunction, clarifying their ignorance, which lies in their falling into contradiction, and emphasizing it, because in their acknowledgment of it there is a wonder that contradicts their state. So: ﴿And if you asked them﴾ also about what is greater than that and more indicative of power, and all the attributes of perfection, and I said to them: ﴿Who created the heavens﴾ with their height and vastness, ﴿and the earth﴾ with the abundance of its wonders and its greatness, ﴿they would surely say﴾ — that is, without hesitation.

Since the question concerned the subject (mubtada'), the matching answer would be the mention of the predicate (khabar). So the answer here would be "Allah," as in other verses, but He turned away from that to a semantic correspondence, diverting the speech away from the manifestation of greatness to the attributes that convey power over everything, and that He, exalted is He, overcomes everything and nothing overcomes Him. The verb is repeated for emphasis on their acknowledgment, increasing their rebuke and alerting them to the magnitude of their error. So He said, expressing by what is necessarily entailed by their acknowledgment of Him, glorified is He, of the sole-ness in origination, because it is the most suitable of things to the aim of the surah and to the clarity which is its opening: 

﴿He created them﴾, who is described as ﴿the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾ — that is, the One who obligates the one who acknowledges that He created these to acknowledge that He overcomes everything and nothing overcomes Him, (p-389) and that His knowledge encompasses everything, so that He is able to originate it in one manner of innovation, then in a more perfect one, then in one more splendid than that, and so on without end. This is the most fitting for the perfection of His essence and the majesty of His attributes. We seek refuge in Allah from the blindness of the Mu'tazilah and the philosophers, the people of rigid minds and stagnant intellects, and from the Arabs' ignorance, for they worship, while acknowledging this, other than Him, and that other has no power over anything at all and no knowledge of anything at all. Thus this question, by its answer, has broken their argument, and their error and disgrace have become evident, until it became clear to people of understanding that they are obstinate.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 10:

Since their answer was not with these two attributes, and mentioning them indicated that they were necessarily acknowledged by them, [He] drew attention to the place of the proof by following these two from His speech, as an indication of that. Here is His saying, turning to direct address because it is more effective in rebuke, reproach and censure, and as a reminder to them of the kindness that requires submission, and as a detailing of the power: ﴿Who has made for you﴾, for if that were their saying they would have said "for us." ﴿The earth a cradle﴾, that is, a bed: firm, stable and spread out. And had He willed, He would have made it shaking, in which nothing stays still, as you see in some mountains, or He would have made it a surface on which nothing is stable because it lies over a current of water. Since He made the earth a resting place for your bodies, He made the bodies a resting place for your souls, and the power to dispose of its resting place and the strength to act with it in their presence (p-390) and their travels, so that this would show you His disposal of the cosmos and His directing of it as He wills, and that He is the Manifest whom nothing exceeds and the Hidden whom nothing conceals. Al-Qushayri said: when the period of the souls' existence on the earth ends, God decrees its ruin; likewise, when the spirits completely separate from the bodies, God decrees their ruin. He repeated the verb as an alert to His exalted ability to establish the causes to facilitate difficult matters, informing that nothing can overcome Him: ﴿and made for you therein roads﴾, that is, paths you travel between the mountains and the valleys. Had He willed, He would have made them such that no one could travel in any place of it, as He made some mountains like that. Then He mentioned the ultimate purpose of that, saying: ﴿so that you may be guided﴾, that is, so that our creating it in this way makes your state that of one who is hoped to be guided to the goals of worldly life in travels and other things, outwardly, so that by them you reach the distant regions and the wide territories for useful, beneficial matters. For when their traversal is repeated, they acquire traces arising from repetition that guide every passer-by to other goals, and to their wisdom (p-391) inwardly, when the discerning one reflects upon the wisdom of the One who subjected them, set them in place and facilitated them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 11:

Since the sending down of water from on high is extremely wondrous, especially when it occurs at one time rather than another, and since the growing of plants by it is even more wondrous, and it is clearly and necessarily a sign of the Resurrection, and since the aim of the surah is that they must be turned from their obstinacy and their greatest ingratitude to faith and to submission to Him with complete acquiescence, He said, indicating the perfection of His power over that and other things by means of the emphasis on perfection of attribute through the conjunction and by repeating the relative pronoun that denotes the masculine agent in His majesty, to point out that the return (to life) of which this is the proof is the secret of existence. It is more noble than what was intended by the preceding verse concerning the cradle of the earth and the threading of paths: ﴿And He who sent down﴾, that is, in gradual measure, and were it not for His overpowering ability, it would have been all at once or nearly so, ﴿from the sky﴾, that is, the lofty place, ﴿water﴾, sweet for your crops, your fruits, your drinking, and for your livestock, ﴿in measure﴾, and it is such that it benefits people and does not harm them, by being in proportion to their needs. He indicated the greatness of the growth by turning the speech to the locus of majesty, to point out that it is the clear proof of what He connected with it of the raising of the dead. So He said, causing this as a consequence: ﴿Then We revived﴾, that is, We gave life, and the root (n-sh-r) revolves around movement, extension and spreading out, ﴿thereby﴾, that is, by the water, ﴿a land﴾, that is, a place where people gather to dwell, caring for its revival and cooperating to maintain its continuance, ﴿dead﴾, that is, its plants had withered and its people were unable to bring water to it so that it might be revived by it. Perhaps He made "land" feminine and "dead" masculine to indicate that its state of weakness and death had reached the utmost limit: by the weakness of its earth in itself, the weakness of its people in reviving it, the dryness of the time, and the vanishing of what plants had been in it.

Since there is no difference between gathering water for plants from the depths of the earth, after it was dust among its dust, and bringing it out as it was, bulging and stirring with life in its form and colors, and what was among its branches as its boughs by God's command, and between God's gathering of what has been scattered from the bodies of the children of Adam and bringing them out as they were, with their spirits and all their substances and accidents; but God is capable in every respect and at every time without any condition at all, and water has no power except by God's decree, it was a great boast to seize the opportunity for the decree of what they deny and disbelieve concerning the matter of the Resurrection. So God said, waking them from their slumber and raising them from the death of their intoxication: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like this great bringing forth of the plants you observe, ﴿you will be brought out﴾ from physical and spiritual death by the easiest of His commands and the simplest of His affairs, ﴿and so you will come out among the dead from the earth a second time﴾ [Ar-Rum: 20] ﴿when, behold, you are human beings spreading abroad﴾ and you will come out of the darkness of ignorance into the light of faith; then you will be wise and knowing.

The translation of this passage follows. Transliterated technical terms are glossed on first occurrence.

When this opportunity was seized, and the mention of it was justified by what their bad belief had produced of great distress, he proceeded to complete what the situation required of the attributes, saying, returning to the style of might and knowledge to hint at urging reflection upon the proof of the resurrection of the dead through the spreading out of the dead earth, and repeating the conjunction to alert to the perfection of that attribute which necessitates the realization of the purpose of the surah, namely the power to return them after their turning away: ﴿And He who created all the pairs﴾, that is, the kinds that are similar, of which none attains complete perfection except through its counterpart, according to what He, glorified is He, has arranged in the systems of this existence, ﴿all of them﴾, from among plants and animals, and other than that from among the rest of the beings; none shared with Him in any of them.

When He mentioned the pairs, and the first thing to come to mind was their application to what is of one single type, this showed that what is meant is what is more general. So He said, mentioning what is similar in carrying and different in body: ﴿And has made for you﴾, not for others, so be thankful to Him, ﴿of the ships﴾, that is, the great vessels on the sea, ﴿and the cattle﴾ on land, ﴿that you ride﴾. The omission of the returning pronoun is for the sake of understanding the meaning, giving precedence to what transitive directly over the cattle (al-an'am) over what transitive through an intermediary in the case of the ship (al-falak), by way of prioritization (taghlib) (the grammatical preference of one term over another in a single construction).

(p-394) When he had mentioned the blessing that arises from bringing things into existence in general, he mentioned the blessing of ease in it, saying, giving the reason: ﴿that you may sit firmly﴾, that is, that you may be in balance, steadiness, stability and comfort ﴿upon their backs﴾, that is, upon the backs of each of those things that were made. The pronoun refers to what is plural in form (al-zahr, "backs"), taking its meaning into account, to multiply the blessing. He used the singular pronoun, "upon its back," in agreement with the wording, to indicate complete power through the great variety of its disposal on land and sea. Or it is a reminder, by the masculine form, of the strength of the mount, since the male is stronger than the female.

When he had completed the blessing by creating everything that need calls for, and had arranged it in a way that points to His attributes, he mentioned what should follow from these blessings, according to what is customary among people: thanking the benefactor. He said, indicating the great worth of the blessing, its exalted purpose, and the exalted status of remembrance, using the particle of delay (thumma): ﴿then you remember﴾, that is, with your hearts. He turned the speech to describing the nurturing, urging remembrance of His kindness so that they would desist from ingratitude and turn to thankfulness. He said: ﴿the blessing of your Lord﴾, who has done good to you by the blessing of subjecting these things to you, and by other blessings you know of.

Since balance upon it is an extraordinary matter, as shown by the fact that animals are not ridden on land and that solid things are not ridden on sea, and although its wonder has fallen away through familiarity with it, he reminded them of it, saying: ﴿when you have settled upon it﴾. Since remembering the blessing (p-395) stirs the heart, the tongue and the limbs to thank the One who bestowed it, he said: ﴿and say﴾, that is, with your tongues, combining heart and tongue. Since settling upon it requires remembering one's deficiency, in needing it to reach what one rides for, in remaining steady upon it, and in fearing destruction from it; and since remembering that He who constantly does good to the weak, who are in His grip from beginning to end, without any return He seeks from them, can only be far from the attributes of baseness; and that His settling upon His Throne is not like this settling accompanied by these deficiencies; and that "there is nothing like unto Him" — the context called for declaring Him free of imperfection (tanzih, the affirmation that God is exalted above all defects). So he said: ﴿Glory be to the One who has subjected﴾, that is, by His perfect knowledge and complete power ﴿this to us﴾, that is, what we ride, whether ship or beast ﴿and we were not﴾, that is, while we were not ﴿capable of it﴾. Since each of the two conveyances is in reality stronger than the rider, he made their inability to master it, and their lack of power over it, as if it were specific to Him. So he said, placing the prepositional phrase first to indicate this: ﴿having the power over it﴾, that is, it was not within our nature to be able to be its match alone, since its strength is beyond what we attempt and strive for, and beyond our capacity, (p-396) in every respect; nor could we be equals in strength, overpowering, controlling, or dominating it. The word muqrinin comes from aqrana al-amr, meaning he became capable of it and was strong enough for it, so that he could bring it under his command as he wished.

When every rider of one of these two kinds of mount constantly recalls that he will return from the far end of his journeys to the place of his settling, Allah (glorified is He) reminded them that the surface of this earth is for them like the backs of ships and beasts, on which they sail through the deep waves of time and the turns of events. They are travellers upon its back, but because of long familiarity with it they are heedless of this and seldom remember it. They are also in danger in what they have come to by means of these things' backs: it is likely to be the cause of their death, the stirrer of their destruction and their power. So He said, connecting (ʿāṭifan) to what is implied: "Then from our Lord came our beginning. We knew nothing and were powerless over nothing. Now we are settled whenever we wish, and spread out whenever we will." ﴿And indeed, to our Lord﴾, the One who does good to us by originating us and by keeping us upon these movements and these mounts, and to no other, ﴿we are surely returning﴾. That is: we are surely heading, turning and travelling, by death and what follows it, to the Last Abode, a return with no coming back from it to this abode. So the verse, through worldly travel, alerts to the otherworldly journey. He emphasised this because of their denial of resurrection, so that they would not cease to be watchful (p-٣٩٧) of the One who bestowed favour upon them. It is also possible that the meaning is: when He commanded them to be mindful of the blessing of riding, He expressed it by "returning", reminding them of His blessing upon them in the state of ease and rest before the return and after it. That is: "And indeed, after our return to the blessing of our Lord, we are returning," i.e., we are in blessing in every state.

Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī (who said: ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ) and al-Nasāʾī narrated from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) that he put his foot in the stirrup and said: "In the name of Allah." When he was firmly seated upon the mount, he said: "Praise be to Allah, who has subjected this to us..." (the verse), then he praised Allah three times and glorified Him three times, then said: "Glory be to You, there is no god but You; I have wronged myself, so forgive me." Then he laughed. He reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) did the same, and said: "The Lord marvels at His servant when he says: 'My Lord, forgive me,' and He says: 'My servant knows that none forgives sins but Me.'"

Aḥmad narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had him ride behind him on a mount. When he was firmly seated upon it, he magnified Allah three times, praised Him three times, glorified Him three times, and declared His oneness once. Then he leaned back upon it and laughed. Then he turned to me and said: "No Muslim man rides his mount and does what I have done without Allah turning towards him, laughing at him as I laughed at you."

Aḥmad, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī and al-Tirmidhī narrated from Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he mounted his riding camel, would say three times, then say: "Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us..." (the verse). Then he would say: "O Allah, I ask You in this journey of mine for righteousness and piety, and for deeds that please You. O Allah, make the journey easy for us and fold up the distance for us. O Allah, You are the Companion on the journey and the Successor over the family. O Allah, accompany us on our journey and be our successor over our family." When he returned to his family, he would say: "Returning, repenting, worshipping, prostrating to our Lord, praising Him, if Allah wills."

Aḥmad narrated from Abū Lāsṭ al-Khuzāʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his family carried us upon camels from the camels of the alms-tax to the Hajj. We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we do not think these should carry us.' He said: 'There is no camel but that on its hump is a devil. So mention the name of Allah over them when you mount them, as He commanded you. Then make them serviceable for yourselves, for it is only Allah, Mighty and Majestic, who carries.'"

When he knew, from this acknowledgment of theirs and the approximation that followed it, that the whole world is paired, with each part subjected to another, it became established that its Creator is distinct from it and that in no way can He be in need, since He has no like at all. The point of wonder was their attribution of offspring to Him, glorified is He. So He said, turning the speech away from their address as a turning-away that signals anger: ﴿And they have made﴾, meaning: and if you asked them, they would say [such-and-such], which necessarily follows, decisively, since He has no like ﴿for Him﴾, while they had attributed to Him, and by their saying before (p-399) your asking them had made, an attribution by which they pass judgment with certainty, admitting no doubt about it, as if they were capable of that, with the capability of one who makes something, ﴿from His servants﴾ whom He originated as He originated others, ﴿a portion﴾, meaning a child. Since they restricted it to the female, it is one of the two kinds of offspring, and everything that is a offspring is a portion of its parent. Whoever has a portion is in need, and so he cannot be a god. This is due to their saying: the angels are daughters of God. Thereby the frivolity of their minds and the feebleness of their opinions became established.

Since this was in the utmost grossness of disbelief, He said, emphasizing against their denial that disbelief is among them: ﴿Indeed, man﴾, meaning this kind of which they are a part, ﴿is truly an ungrateful one, manifest﴾, meaning one who makes disbelief manifest in himself, proclaiming it openly, making it clear to everyone. This is what his nature requires, given his deficiency through desires and self-interests, so that the excellence of the one whom God has preserved with intellect over all other creatures is made clear, through his striving against an enemy that lies between his two sides, together with the manifest display of God's dazzling power in that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 16:

Since it is as if it were said, in denial against them and in mockery of them, that they were not content to make for Him, who has the making, from among His servants a part, until they made it the worse of the two parts, the females, although they are the most averse of people to them: that part which you have made females was given to Him, apart from it, by compulsion, such that He could not be free of it, as He mentioned in the surah before it (p-400) concerning His Holy Self, that He bestows females upon whomever He wills and cannot fall short of them in any way. He matched it with His saying, returning to address them, because it is more effective in rebuking them for choosing error over right: ﴿Or has He taken﴾, meaning He Himself treated and then took after the treatment, while He is the Creator of all creation, ﴿of what He creates﴾, meaning He renews His origination at every moment, as you acknowledged, ﴿daughters﴾. So He did not, after the burden and the toil, settle for anything other than daughters, which are the more hateful of the two parts to you. He used the indefinite form to specify that His taking was of a portion of this category, in which others share with Him. He conjoined it to His saying "taken" so that the negation would be in the most eloquent manner, since it lies within the scope of denial: ﴿and has chosen for you﴾, while He is the Master and you are His servants, ﴿the sons﴾, meaning the more perfect part in your estimation, the one deserving to be always present in the mind. For this reason He made it definite. And because they claimed that this entire category belongs exclusively to them, and that He shares none of it with them, this second disbelief was more deeply rooted in impossibility than the first, since it adds to the absolute need the folly of being content with the base and despicable, while assigning to Himself none of the exalted, and instead making that exalted portion for them purely and cleansed of the least of what might mar it of turbidity.

The attribution of a child to Him, glorified is He, is something that should never occur to the mind under any circumstances. Its attribution to Him in literal reality is even farther removed than in the sense of illustration, by saying: "The angels, in His presence, hold the status of daughters in the sight of a father." He (Allah) said, guiding to the fact that what they said, even if intended as an illustration (tamthil, a comparison), is extremely ugly, let alone if it were meant as an established fact. This returns to the turning away that signals hatred and distance: ﴿And when﴾, meaning, they made this attribution while the situation is that when ﴿one of them is given good news﴾ from whatever bearer of news it may be, ﴿of that which he has struck﴾, the phrase ﴿of that which he has struck﴾ is an alert that it is among the things that please, like a male, both being a child, and at times it pleases and at other times it displeases, and it is a blessing from the Creator, because it is better than barrenness. He turned away from the description with lordship (rububiyyah) because one may claim a share in general nurturing, to the description that indicates the generality of mercy. Reflect on this: by itself it is sufficient as a deterrent against the evil of their statement. So He said: ﴿to the Most Merciful﴾, meaning the One for whom there is no blessing on any of creation except that it comes from Him, ﴿a likeness﴾, meaning He assigned to Him a resemblance, which is the female. He expressed it this way rather than saying "that which He made," in the place of "that which he has struck," as a teaching of courtesy regarding His glory in this surah, whose purpose is knowledge that necessitates courtesy, and as an increase in condemning their disbelief, especially if they intended the literal reality, by indicating that a child cannot be other than like its parent, and it is not conceivable at all that it should be outside its likeness in its particular attributes. [p-402] Since a change of the face, especially to blackness, is not fully perceived except in daylight, He expressed it with what is literally used for continuance during the day, although the intended meaning here is continuance in general: ﴿becomes﴾, meaning remains, ﴿his face darkened﴾, meaning intensely black, due to the aversion he finds, which leads to rage, at this news which experience has shown may be pleasing. ﴿And he is clenched with grief﴾, meaning he restrains himself, filled with distress. So how can a reasonable person disdain something and yet be content to attribute it to His servant, let alone to his equal, let alone to his master? This is something no reasonable person would be content to pass through his thought, let alone to utter.

Since the king takes into his army only those who are fit for soldiering, through strength in combat, argument, or one of the two, He drew attention to another denial: that females are not fit for either of these two qualities. So He said, making the denial of the third a tool for highlighting that it is extremely provocative of anger: ﴿Is one who is raised up in ornaments﴾, meaning, one whom they have taken for themselves while they would not accept such a thing for themselves, and who has taken for Himself one who is ﴿raised up﴾, that is, according to what your customs have been, in the reading of the majority (al-Jama'ah), and whom you raise and adorn with your effort, in the reading with a dammah on the ba' and a shaddah on the shin, ﴿in ornaments﴾, that is, in adornment, so that she is a burden upon her father, unfit for war, nor for dealing with spear-thrust or blow, ﴿and she﴾ (p-403), that is, while the state is that she, and He placed first, for the sake of emphasis, His saying, ﴿in dispute﴾, when it is needed, ﴿is not clear﴾, that is, there does not come from her a complete, absolute clarification of what she intends, due to deficiency of intellect and weakness of judgment, through the clash of desires and appetites and the dominance of softness, so there is no defense from her by hand or by tongue.

Al-Biqa'i's commentary (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 19:

Since one might think the forbidden matter is only their making the angels, upon them be peace, females by attributing them to Him, may He be glorified, he draws attention to the fact that this is abhorrent in itself without qualification, because it indicates contempt for them and belittling of them. So it is a third kufr added to the two kufrs before it: ascribing a child to Him, may He be glorified. Then he specified the more particular of the two types, saying: ﴿And they made﴾, i.e., being bold toward what no intelligent person should do, ﴿the angels, who are﴾ characterized by the most noble attributes, ﴿the servants of the All-Merciful﴾, the one of universal blessing, who created them. So they are among those who worship Him, and they are His servants in truth, because they have not disobeyed Him for the blink of an eye, so they are fit to be in the most perfect states. The reading "ʿinda" (ﻋِﻨْﺪَ, "in the presence of") with a nūn is a strong proclamation of their foolishness, because the people of the king's court, whom he employs in important matters, are only in the most perfect states, and "his presence" means that they never disobeyed him at all. They are a sanctified place, far from sins, honored with acts of obedience and with those chosen for distinction. (p-404) The second object of "made" is mentioned in the sense of belief and assertion, so he said: ﴿females﴾. That is the lowest of attributes in creation, essence, and quality. Then he indicated their lie in this unqualified claim, to show their lie in the qualified claim a fortiori. So he said, mocking them, rebuking them, and denouncing them, to show the corruption of their minds: that their claims are bare of evidence: ﴿Did they witness﴾, i.e., were they present, in a presence in which they had complete knowledge, outwardly and inwardly. This is the meaning of the reading of the majority. Nafiʿ introduced an interrogative hamza (hamzat al-tawbīkh, the hamza of reproach, ﺃ) before another hamza, which was pronounced with a ḍamma and with the verb in the passive, to indicate their inability to witness that except by one who makes them witness it, and that is the Creator and no other. Its lengthening in one of the two transmissions is an increase in the material against them with disgrace. He made the second hamza easier by placing it between itself and the waw, as a sign of the lowliness of their affair, the baseness of their opinions and actions, and all their changes and states, as time and the calamities of events will reveal. ﴿Their creation﴾, i.e., the act of creation in its origin, or at birth, or after it, in some state of the states, a presence that made it necessary for them to realize what they said, in that they were not absent from any of the states that indicate that. This is more general than whether that witnessing is sensory by seeing with the eye, or immaterial by necessary knowledge, or inferential by reason or by revelation.

Since the answer is definitely "No," he said, threatening them and emphasizing his threat (p-405) with the sīn (ﺳَ), because they thought there would be no resurrection, no reckoning, no gathering, and no dispersal. So he said: ﴿Their testimony will be recorded﴾, by the writing of those whom We appointed over them, of the guardians who do not disobey Us, for We empower them over everything We command them. This is according to the reading of the majority, with the tāʾ and the passive voice. The greatness of the writing is for magnifying the threat and exalting what it contains of menace, in the reading with the nūn, which implies greatness, and the active voice. He put the testimony in the accusative: ﴿their testimony﴾, i.e., their statement about them that they are females, which should not be made except after complete witnessing. So it is a feeble, foolish, weak statement, as the feminine form in the reading of the majority indicates. ﴿And they will be questioned﴾ about it when they return to Us. It is possible that the sīn contains an appeal to repentance before the writing and before they have knowledge of it. For Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him, related that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

"The recorder of good deeds is on the right of the man, and the recorder of bad deeds is on the left of the man. The recorder of good deeds is trustworthy over the recorder of bad deeds. When he does a good deed, the one on the right writes it ten times; when he does a bad deed, the one on the right says to the one on the left: 'Leave him for seven hours, perhaps he will glorify Allah or seek forgiveness.'" Narrated by al-Shaʿbi, and al-Baghawi from his route, and al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi from the route of Jaʿfar, from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah; and al-Bayhaqi from the narration of Bishr ibn Numayr from al-Qasim similarly; and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Ḥilya; and Ibn Mardawayh (p-406) from the route of Ismaʿil ibn ʿAyyash, from ʿAsim ibn Rajaʾ, from ʿUrwah ibn Ruwaym, from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Hakim also related, and said: "Its isnad is sound," from Umm ʿIsmah al-ʿUwsiyyah, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with her, who said: "No Muslim commits a sin except that the king pauses for three hours. If he seeks forgiveness for his sin, it is not recorded against him, and he is not punished on the Day of Resurrection."

When he mentioned that they would be asked, a fortiori, about their worship, he drew attention to the fact that they worshipped the angels while claiming that the angels were female. So he said, marvelling at them for this, and at their making their own statement a proof confirming the correctness of their position, which is among the weakest of doubts: ﴿And they say﴾, that is, after their worship of them and their prohibition of worship other than God: ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾, that is, the One who possesses all-encompassing mercy. [They argued this] because all-encompassing mercy prevents Him from permitting what is not fitting. But He did not will that we should not worship them, so we worship them by the leave of His will. Therefore our worship of them is a truth. Had it not been a truth that He approves of for us, He would have hastened the punishment upon us.

Since it was as if it had been said, "With what will they be answered regarding this?", he said, drawing attention to their answer and indicating by his words that the foundations of the religion (uṣūl al-dīn, the fundamental principles of faith) may not be spoken about except with certainty: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾ (p-407), that is, of this far-fetched meaning, distant from correctness, which they intended to make a proof of the validity of their worship of them, namely that He, glory be to Him, wills only what is true and approves it and commands it; and [they have no knowledge] that the angels are female. He emphasised the comprehensiveness of the negation with the words ﴿any knowledge﴾, that is, because if this followed, then His placing [the angels] under the all-encompassing mercy would necessarily be compulsory rather than voluntary, which leads to deficiency rather than perfection. It would also lead to the necessity that all people be approved of by Him, since they would be upon the truth, and that undoubtedly leads to the two contradictories both being true at once, which is manifestly impossible.

Since knowledge may be absent while the known thing is established in itself, he said, negating that: ﴿They are only guessing﴾, that is, they are only lying in this conclusion which they claimed showed them God's pleasure with their disbelief, glory be to Him. For it is based on the premise that He, glory be to Him, wills only what is true. What emboldened them to this was that they continually renew speech without verification or careful examination, so most of what they say is false. Thus they became bold in deliberately saying things on the basis of conjecture, which does not protect its holder from falling into a plain falsehood. The full refutation of this doubt will come in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of those who worship [him]﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81], and that this is what is meant, not what the discourse has wandered into through neglect of the preceding and following matters that necessitate the arrangement of the speech, fitting the requirement of the situation. (p-408) In this statement they have displayed several ignorances: the claim of sonship for the absolutely Self-Sufficient; that offspring is the lower of the two categories; their worship of beings who are, by themselves, inferior to them, without any proof; their reliance, for the validity of their act, on a supposed knowledge which He has forbidden them through the tongue of every messenger; and their assumption that He wills only what is true, which leads to the joining of the two contradictories together, since there is no doubt about this and no concealment in it.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 21:

Since belief in the angels (*malā'ikah*), who are the soldiers of the King, is one of the pillars of the fundamentals of the religion (*uṣūl al-dīn*), and since belief in a thing is defective if it is not in accordance with what that thing actually is, even in its least aspect, God, glory be to Him, informed that they described the angels otherwise than they are. They fell short by describing them as daughters, to the point of degrading them to the lowest level, and they went to excess in worship, to the point of raising them above their rank. In both respects they departed from clear reason (*ṣarīḥ al-ʿaql*), as indicated by what has preceded. He then followed this with the point that they are also devoid of sound transmission (*ṣaḥīḥ al-naql*). So He said, in parallel with His words ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ (43:19), as a further denunciation of them after a denunciation, making this carry the greatest shame: diverting the speech away from the attribute of mercy, to draw attention through the manifestation of majesty, to the effect that when His judgment becomes manifest, no hearer may do anything but stop before it and comply in every state, or else the greatest punishment will befall him: ﴿Or have We given them﴾ (by what belongs to Us of majesty) ﴿a Book﴾, that is, one comprehensive of what they wish to hold as belief from these sayings of theirs, ﴿before it﴾, that is, before the Qur'an, in which We informed them that We made the angels females, and that We do not will except what is true, which We are pleased with and which We command. ﴿So they﴾, that is, as a consequence of this giving, ﴿by it﴾, that is, by it alone, ﴿are holding fast﴾, that is, they are establishing firm adherence to it and seeking to remain steadfast upon it in the worship of other than God. There is also in this that it is true, since He did not hasten to punish them, and in their describing the angels with femaleness, and in everything else of all that they commit of falsehood. The denial (*inkār*) requires the negation of what the denial is applied to, namely the giving of a Book, just as the making them witness the creation of the angels has been negated. This parallel, about which no one who has insight into speech has any doubt, indicates the soundness of the view that the reference in ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾ (43:20) includes their claim of femaleness regarding the angels.

Since the answer was to cut off these two interrogations, namely: "They have no such claim, neither on the basis of any unrestricted nor restricted statement, nor on the basis of clear reason or sound transmission from those scholars of the divine reports whose transmission is reliable," He linked to it, as a guide towards it, His saying: ﴿Nay, they say﴾, that is, in their answer concerning that saying and belief, emphatically, showing either ignorance or feigned ignorance, because that was only blamed upon them due to their assumption that there was no predecessor for them at all in this matter. So when it is established that it came from those who preceded them, the dispute is settled: (p-410) ﴿"Indeed, we found our fathers﴾, that is, and they were superior to us in intellects and sounder in understanding, ﴿upon a community﴾, that is, a great way of life that deserves to be aimed at and followed, like a journey, meaning a thing worthy of being traveled towards, and likewise a model and the like.

The reading with the kasra (ʾimma, "a community" read as ʾimmah) means a good condition that deserves to be followed: ﴿and indeed we are upon their traces﴾, that is, specifically, not upon anything else, and we are in the utmost striving and tracing of the traces, even if we do not find a concrete thing to verify.

When He knew this from their condition, and it was not explicit in indicating guidance, they specified the prepositional phrase and the object, and they reported after the report and drew from it their saying, as a resumption answering one who asks: ﴿guided﴾, that is, we ourselves. So when it is established by this emphatic statement that we have not brought anything from our own selves, nor erred in following and tracing the traces, then there is no objection against us in any respect. This is their saying concerning religion, indeed concerning its foundations, in which whoever goes astray in any of them is ruined. And if there appeared to any of them a flaw in the worldly endeavour of his father, by which he acquires the dinar and the dirham, he would not have followed him at all and would have opposed him in whatever opposition; this is nothing but pure desire and shortness of vision, and he made his destination the present worldly matter, with no authority for them in meanings in any respect.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 23:

When the abandoning of the one who is called to the proof, and the following of his own whims, was something enraging, painful, irritating and grievous, He said, consoling His Prophet ﷺ, linking it to His words: ﴿And thus﴾ (p-411), that is, and in the same manner as this most abominable act, the earlier nations did with their brother prophets, upon them be prayer and peace. Then He explained that by His words: ﴿We did not send﴾, together with what belongs to Us of greatness.

Since the saying of Quraysh had already preceded, and the intended purpose was consolation through others, and since he ﷺ was the Seal of the Prophets, so that there was no community other than his in his time or after him to console him with, He consoled him with those who had passed away. He placed the mention of the "qiblah" (the prior period, i.e., the preceding ones) first, showing concern for the consolation and purifying it from the suspicion that there might be with him in his time or after him a warner. It also conveys that the renewer of His law is only a helper to his community and a bringer of good tidings, not a warner, for the steadfastness of his community upon the religion through their affirming all the prophets. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿before you﴾, that is, in the bygone eras, even those very close to you, for consolation through the nearest is greater. He affirmed the preposition because sending in the verbal sense did not encompass all eras. He omitted this "before" in *Saba'* because the intended meaning there is generality, since no mention of Quraysh had preceded so as to specify those before them. Since the people of the towns are closer to reason and more worthy of wisdom and wise sayings, He said: ﴿in a town﴾, and He emphasized the negation with His words: ﴿any warner﴾, and by it He made clear that the point of aversion and dispute is warning against opposing desires. ﴿But its affluent ones said﴾, that is, the people of luxury (*taraffuh*, with a *ḍamma*), which is blessing, good food, and a pleasant thing that is specific to the affluent. That necessitates laxity, and it necessitates ease and idleness (p-412), diverting one from the effort of striving toward the baseness of imitation; it necessitates inclining to whims even when the proof is clear; it necessitates rebellion and persistence in it, obstinacy in it, arrogance and tyranny. Most people, for the most part, are followers of these: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers﴾, that is, while they know better than us about matters, ﴿upon a community﴾, that is, a unified matter deserving to be aimed at and followed, a way and a religion. They emphasized it to cut off any hope of the dissenter turning them away from that: ﴿and indeed we are upon their traces﴾, not other than them. Then they specified the prepositional phrase and gave a second predicate, and they resumed to complete their meaning, saying, for clarification, since the cause of the narrative is exemplary conduct: ﴿following﴾, that is, emulating, that is, riding the paths of their way, adhering to it, because they are those who are followed, so that one goes before them. And our state is the best it can be in uprightness, nearer and swifter.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 24:

When it was as if it had been said, "So every warner said, 'What am I to do?'", he answered with his words, "Say" (qul), meaning, "O warner" — this is according to the reading of the majority (al-Jama'ah). According to the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Hafs and 'Asim, the implied meaning is that the listener said, "What did the warner say in reply to them?" So he was answered with His words, "He said," in denial of them: ﴿Even if﴾, meaning, "Would you follow your fathers in every circumstance and consider them rightly guided, even if ﴿I brought you﴾" — and the pronoun (p-413) in it refers to the warner. In the reading of Abu Ja'far it is: "Even if I brought you of the warners, all of them" ﴿with a better guidance﴾, meaning, a matter greater in guidance and clearer in indication, ﴿than that which you found﴾, meaning, O you who follow your fathers, ﴿your fathers upon it﴾. This is because your saying includes that you follow their traces in the greatest of matters, which is the religion, where loss is a loss of the soul, while you oppose them in worldly affairs when you find a path better than their way of managing them, even in a small matter; and one of you boasts that he has attained what his father did not attain, so that he acquired more wealth than he acquired. How strange is such a view, how short-sighted it is, and how ruinous is such a trade!

Since it was known that the warners said to them what they were commanded to say, the listener eagerly awaited their reply to them, so he was answered with His words: ﴿They said﴾, emphatically, in refutation of what every intelligent person who heard this speech would be certain of — that they would hasten to examine the proof and return to the right path: ﴿Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which you have been sent﴾, meaning, O you who claim to be sent, from whatever sender it may be, even if what you claim of messengerhood were established, and even if you brought us something better. ﴿Disbelievers﴾, meaning, concealers: our effort is to conceal what appears of that, so that it does not become apparent to anyone and no created being follows them in it.

When he knew this, that their affair had reached obstinacy which nullifies argument, he made the following statement a consequence of it, as an admonition to this community and an explanation of the mercy with which He singled it out: ﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾, that is, by what We possess of the majesty which they deserved, ﴿from them﴾, so We destroyed them with the punishment of annihilation. The effect of the retribution is magnified by the command to contemplate it in His saying: ﴿So look﴾, that is, by way of seeking knowledge of that, and by way of the interrogative, indicating that this is a matter whose cause is, because of its magnitude, worthy of being hidden. So He said: ﴿how was the end of those who denied﴾, that is, the final outcome of those who denied Our sending. For they were all destroyed, and all the believers were saved. So let whoever rejects your message beware of the like of that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 26:

When he had mentioned to them the proofs and warned them against taking (the path of their fathers), and it became clear that they, along with imitation (taqlid), would never be free of it, he reminded them of the greatest of their fathers, the focus of their pride and the most deserving of following, so that they might win by following the father in abandoning imitation, or in imitating him if imitation were unavoidable for them, because he was the greatest of fathers and because his (position) was accompanied by proof. So He said, conjoining (this) to what is implied in its presumed sense, to draw attention to his reflection and deep consideration of it: "Recount to them that." That is: and recount to them the time when ﴿Ibrahim (Abraham)﴾, the greatest of their fathers, the focus of their pride, and the one agreed upon by them, the People of the Book and others, to be beloved and to have a true religion, ﴿said to his father﴾ without imitating him as you have imitated your fathers. And since opposing the many is severe for one person, He mentioned his state in this regard as a clarification, because they are more deserving than them of being freed from imitation. ﴿and to his people﴾, who were in reality the (true) people, since they comprised possession of all the earth, as I have said: "Indeed we are for you equal." And since they could not imagine at all that anyone would oppose them, he emphasized with the particle and the manifest nun of protection, and so He said: ﴿Indeed I﴾, and he increased (the emphasis) by the description with the verbal noun, which is the same for the singular and others, and the masculine and others, because it is a verbal noun, even though it occupies the position of an adjective, with a word that indicates that he is embodied in disavowal, making it in the form of the intensified pattern for greater emphasis, and so He said: ﴿innocent (bara')﴾. Whoever reads it with a damma makes it a pure adjective, like tuwal in tawil. ﴿of what you worship﴾, in the present and future, whatever it may be, excepting whoever was an exception, for they were polytheists; so there must be an exception, and it must be a connected one. Imam Abu 'Ali al-Hasan ibn Yahya ibn Nasr al-Jurjani said in his book Bayan Nuzum al-Qur'an, in substance: The secret of the saying of the early generation that "the word" here, that is the verse, in His saying "a word that remains" ("la ilaha illa Allah"), is that negation and disavowal are one; for "Indeed I am innocent (bara')" is in the place of "la" (no), and His saying ﴿of what you worship﴾ is in the place of "ilah" (god), since every object of worship is called a god.

So this comes back to: ﴿There is no god except He who originated me﴾. He said: By this interpretation I have joined to your first understanding, which you derived from the report, the true knowledge (*ma'rifah haqiqiyyah*) that your nature was led to through reflection. By describing Him with *fiṭar* (origination), he drew attention to the proof of his belief, namely that He who split non-existence (*al-'adam*) and brought me forth from it, then formed these faculties of perception and cognition, and whoever has this overwhelming power is singular in greatness.

Since God, glory be to Him, and to Him belongs all favor, had bestowed, after bringing into existence, what he indicated of intellect and senses, which prepare one for guidance without any request, it was fitting that He grant the one who seeks Him the greatest guidance. He said, as a consequence of his severing his attachments to anyone other than Him, emphasizing it for the sake of one who denies that he could reach a level that his forebears were blind to: ﴿Indeed He will guide me﴾. That is, guidance which is the guidance to the realities that have become clear to me, [guidance] to everything that makes me fit to turn toward Him and rely upon Him. I have no doubt in this belief. By this phrase, connected with the *sin* (of future time), he conveyed his guidance in the future, after he had conveyed, in his saying related in al-Shu'ara', ﴿It is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:78], guidance in the present. It seems he specified this with the *sin* because of what followed it of its consequences, so he made their guidance his guidance.

﴿And He made it﴾, that is, Abraham, peace be upon him, made this word, which is monotheism (tawhid) with its proof, ﴿a word lasting among his descendants﴾, that is, his offspring. He supplicated, and his supplications were answered, in His saying: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], and in His saying ﴿and [make] from my descendants﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], and ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom and purify them. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. ﴿So that they might return﴾, that is, so that their condition would be like that of one who looks at them: if deviation and crookedness occur among them, they are like one whose return is hoped for. For when they recall that their great father, who built the House for them and bequeathed to them their pride, said this, they would follow him. It is also permissible that it be connected to what "idh" (when) is connected to, meaning: mention to them the saying of their father, so that their condition, in the eyes of one who is ignorant of the outcomes, would be like that of one whose return is hoped for, from the imitation (taqlid) of the ignorant forefathers to following this father, whose following is not considered imitation, because of the proofs that stand behind his saying, which are beyond counting, and so it guarantees for its follower, necessarily, complete victory. And in his phrasing with "hoped for" (la'alla) there is an indication that they would be of two kinds: one kind that returns, and another that does not return. (p. 417)

Since it is known that the listener, having in mind those whose inner and outer states are encompassed by his knowledge, says: "My Lord! Rather, they have turned back," He is answered with His saying: ﴿Rather﴾, meaning: they did not turn back; rather, they persisted, for the sake of My manifesting My power over hearts by casting their lords into the most abominable calamities and the most heinous sins, by their own consent and choice, abandoning the unassailable path and the straightest way, and deviating from it with a great deviation. They persisted in their error and bewilderment, and I did not hasten to punish them, because I ﴿have given enjoyment﴾, the verb being in the singular with His own pronoun (subhanahu), because enjoyment (al-tamti') includes prolonging life, which none can grant, outwardly or inwardly, except Him. As for retribution, He may place it in the hands of His servants, from among the angels and others, and so it falls under ﴿We shall lead them step by step from where they do not know﴾ [al-Qalam: 44] and ﴿And I give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-Qalam: 45]. (p. 418) ﴿These﴾, that is, those present before you of the polytheists and enemies of the religion, ﴿and their fathers﴾. So I extended their lives along with the soundness of their bodies and the firmness of their frames, the abundance of blessings, and their exemption from afflictions and vengeance. Thus My blessings made them insolent, and the bounties of My generosity and munificence made them indifferent, and their riding of that falsehood continued with them ﴿until the truth came to them﴾ with this firm religion, ﴿and a clear messenger﴾. That is, his command is manifest in itself; had there been no clear signs in it, it would have been self-evident, informing you of the news, and it, along with its manifestness in itself, is a manifestation of every meaning they need. And ﴿I have given enjoyment﴾ is spoken in address from the tongue of the Messenger to whom this Book was sent, because he supplicates, seizing the opportunity, perhaps he will be answered with what removes the distress, saying: "My Lord! You have set them up for one who is ignorant of the consequences, in the station of one whose return is hoped for, so You did not decree that, rather You gave enjoyment..." to the end.

Since the sense requires it, the reasoning is: the intended meaning is that the abundance of blessings granted to them, and Our hastening of them to those people, did not turn them back, even though the matter was clear to them. Rather, the bestowal of favour upon them became a cause of their insolence (baṭar), and insolence became a cause of their persistence in using Our blessing to disobey Our command, while they claimed to be the people most devoted to the truth and most restrained from falsehood. Then He joined to this His words ﴿And when the truth came to them﴾, meaning the truth that is perfect in its truthfulness, corresponding to reality without any confusion or ambiguity, and manifest in its perfection to everyone who has even a little intellect, through the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an in its composition, and through what it calls to of wisdom in all its aspects, and through its agreement with what they know of the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, before they altered it, and of the teaching of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them, concerning monotheism (tawhid). Along with that heedlessness, to which insolence over the blessing had led them, they added something worse, which is denial. So they said, out of stubbornness, obstinacy, injustice and rebellion, without pausing or reflecting: ﴿This﴾, pointing to the truth which reality corresponds to, so that nothing is more established than it, namely the Qur'an and what else he brought of the proofs of recognition, ﴿is sorcery﴾, meaning an illusion with no reality. Since the situation required, without doubt or hesitation, that they recognised what he brought and submitted to it, they said, emphasising their opposition to it with what was firmly established in their souls on this matter: ﴿and indeed we are disbelievers in it﴾, meaning that they were deeply immersed in concealing it specifically, so that no one would know it and it would have no follower.

When he had reported their attacks on the Qur'an, he followed it with a report of their attacks on the one who brought it, covering up his affair. This was in line with what he had reported at the end of the preceding passage about their disbelief in themselves, adding to it and going further in what the blessings had led them to in insolence. So He said: ﴿And they said﴾ when what they had been reminded of had overwhelmed them, from what they knew about the affair of Abraham, upon him be prayers and peace, regarding prophethood and messengerhood, and likewise about his descendants after him. Thus they could not sustain their persistence in obstinacy by denying that the Prophet could be a human being. Instead, the statement came from one who holds great authority in disposing of existence and exercising command over the King, who "is not questioned about what He does." So they denied the specification of what they had been given by the specification in their words: ﴿Why not﴾, meaning, "Why not, and why was it not?"

Since the sending down of the Qur'an was in installments according to gradual progression, they expressed it in words that match this, and said: ﴿was sent down﴾, meaning from the one who was sent down, whom Muhammad (ﷺ) had mentioned. They specified their intended meaning and removed ambiguity, and they said, with harshness and a coarse expression toward the one who sought to guide them to amend their state: ﴿this Qur'an﴾, meaning, the one that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought and claimed encompasses every good. In this there is an indication of belittling it. ﴿upon a man from the two towns﴾, meaning Makkah and al-Ta'if. He did not say "one of" (iḥda), being content with the singularity of "a man." ﴿great﴾, meaning by what they regarded as greatness in him: rank, status, wealth, age, and the like. They knew that the proper course of a king is to send one whom they approve of, not one whom the subjects propose. They also knew that the sending king possesses absolute wealth, yet they were ignorant, although he is the one who bestowed wealth and status, that he urged detachment from both and renunciation of them, and that nothing brings one near to him except sincere turning toward him, arising from purity of soul, sharpness of character, perfection of disposition, adornment with all virtues, and freedom from every vice.
