Thus, in their extreme ignorance, they made the bestial state a condition for reaching the angelic state, which is opposed to it in every respect.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 32:

When their statement implied that they claimed greatness for themselves by objecting to the King, He said, rebuking them and denouncing them, with a meaning along the lines of: the matter is not referred back to them, nor is it contingent upon them, but it belongs to Allah alone: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. ﴿Do they﴾, that is, these ignorant and incapable people, ﴿apportion﴾, that is, continually and habitually. He turned the speech from the singular pronoun to the attribute of mercy attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ), honouring him and showing the loftiness of his rank: ﴿the mercy of your Lord﴾, that is, the generosity of the One who benefits you and bestows favour upon you, honours you with all kinds of kindness and goodness, and magnifies you by what He has nurtured in you, by singling you out for the mission to them, qualifying them for rescue from error, and making you, though you are the best of the worlds, the Messenger to them. They were given preference through your excellence, although you are the most noble of them in lineage, the most excellent of them in descent, the greatest of them in intellect, the purest of them in understanding, and the most merciful of them in heart, so that they might dispose of that mercy, which is the spirit of existence and the secret of the matter, according to their desires, while they are not able to dispose of the passing goods in the same way.

Since He had negated that any share of the apportioning belonged to them, He said, answering one who seemed to say: "Who then apportions?", indicating their distance from having any share in what He prepared for their religions, as they witness their distance from the apportioning of what He prepared for their bodies, and turning the speech away from the attribute of beneficence to the locus of greatness, to indicate that greatness rejects sharing in anything and requires singularity: ﴿We have apportioned﴾, that is, by what greatness bestows, ﴿among them﴾, that is, in the matter that encompasses them all and necessitates that each of them be singled out with what is in his possession, ﴿their livelihood﴾, which they count as mercy and confine favour to, ﴿in the life of this world﴾, which is the lowest of things in Our sight. He indicated that it is a deficient life that no intelligent person would be content with. As for the Hereafter, He described it as "the life" (al-hayawan), because if We left its apportioning to them, they would cooperate in that and none of them would remain, so how could it enter the imagination that a share of speech about prophethood, which is the spirit of existence and by which the happiness of both abodes is achieved, be placed in their hands? ﴿And We raised﴾ by the authority of Our command ﴿some of them﴾, even if one of them is weak in body and little in intellect, ﴿above others﴾, even if another is strong and mighty in intellect, ﴿in degrees﴾, in standing, wealth, authority of command, and greatness of rank, so that the state of existence might be ordered. For its order necessarily requires that those who exist share and cooperate. We made them differ among themselves in bodies, powers and aspirations, so that they might divide the crafts, the knowledges and the goods, each being facilitated for what he was created for and inclined to what it is for him to pursue. So no one, whether lowly or rich, is able to exceed his measure [p. 423] or rise above his station.

When He mentioned that, He gave its reason, the fruit of which is the cultivation of the earth, saying: ﴿that they may take﴾, that is, with the utmost of their effort, ﴿some of them some others﴾ as ﴿servants﴾ (sukhriyyan). Since the intended meaning here is employment rather than mockery, as the reason cannot properly be attached to mockery, the reciters (qurra', i.e., the readers of the Qur'an) agreed on the dammah on this letter here, and He said: ﴿sukhriyyan﴾ (servants/subjected), that is, that one uses the other in what befalls him, or what is difficult or impossible for him to do directly, and takes from the other some of the wealth that he needs. So this one has his wealth and that one has his labour. The poor man may even be more perfect than the rich, so that the order of the world may be completed, for if measures were equal, livelihoods would be disrupted. No one is able to separate himself from what We have placed under his control of this lowly matter. How then do they hope to object in the matter of prophethood? Can any intelligent person imagine that We would entrust the apportioning of the inferior while leaving the exalted to others? Ibn al-Jawzi said: "If livelihoods are by the decree of Allah and not by the power of the schemer, and they are less than prophethood, how then can prophethood be?" End of quotation. This is what is meant by the words of the Exalted, turning the speech away from the locus of greatness and sovereignty to the description of beneficence, to show the nobility of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿and the mercy of your Lord﴾, that is, the One who nurtures you and manages your affair by sending you and illuminating existence with your message, which by its greatness is worthy of being attributed to Him, and no one other than you is called mercy. ﴿is better than what they amass﴾ of the perishing debris. For although goodness may be found in it by using it in the ways of righteousness under its conditions, this is in comparison to prophethood, and whatever accompanies us [p. 424] of what calls to turning away from the world is vanishing.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 43, verse 33:

When the explicit sense of the verse of enjoyment (al-tamtī') and the allusion of what follows it showed that expansion in provision, which brings elevation, even though it is of lowly rank and deficient in measure, necessarily takes one out of equality, and the estimation was: "So We single out this good for individuals, in every era, the rare ones among the righteous, that through them We may rescue whomever We will from error, and We give the debris to the arrogant, the base rabble, as a trial for the servants, so that He may make clear to them the people of transgression from the people of right guidance; and were it not for what Our wisdom required by arranging this existence upon causes, with differences among people for the existence to subsist, We would have made them equal." He joined to it His saying, reminding of His gentleness toward the believers and His kindness to them by removing from them what would require, for them, severe striving, great steadfastness and heavy endurance, for a state in which feet slip from the paths of guidance through inclination and attention toward the sources of wealth, kingship, complete power and greatness: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community﴾, i.e., the people who enjoy wealth, with what they have of turbulence and of contentment with themselves, ﴿[they would be] one community﴾, i.e., in misguidance through disbelief, because they would believe that Our giving wealth is evidence of Our love for the one to whom We give it, due to their love of this world and their making it the focus of their gazes and aspirations, except those whom Allah protects; ﴿We would have made﴾, i.e., in every time and every place, by virtue of Our greatness, which no one can oppose, because of the worthlessness of this world in Our sight and Our hatred of it (p-425) ﴿for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾. His saying ﴿in the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., the One whose mercy is all-encompassing, is evidence of the worthlessness of this world in that it is given to the distant and the detested, and that the attribute of mercy would necessitate the utmost extension of blessings upon the disbeliever, were it not for the reason He mentioned, namely kindness toward the believers.

Since the adornment of a container is always according to the adornment of what it contains, this indicates what they have of garments, mounts and other matters, by the adornment of dwellings. So He said, substituting for ﴿for those who﴾ (a substitution of inclusion, since its arrangement by way of substitution is more striking): ﴿for their houses﴾, i.e., which they inhabit, ﴿roofs﴾, i.e., this kind (in the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, with the singular, as evidenced by the reading of the rest with two damm-s as a plural) ﴿of silver﴾, as if He singled it out for the light it gives, ﴿and stairways﴾, i.e., of silver, which are the ascending steps of a staircase, because walking upon them is like the walk of one who is lame, ﴿upon which they ascend﴾, i.e., they rise and climb upon their backs toward the heights.

"And for their houses, doors [of silver] as well."

Since the singular "couch" (sarīr) might give the impression that there is one couch which is turned around for everyone, it is put in the plural so that it is understood that each one has his own couch from among the couches (al-usrah), unlike the roof, for it does not give that impression. Perhaps it was recited with the singular and the plural, so He said: "and couches" in the plural alone, and it indicates the tranquility of their minds and the serenity of their times and conditions with His saying: ﴿upon which they recline﴾. (p-426)

﴿وزُخْرُفًا﴾, meaning gold and general, complete adornment.

Since the word *zukhruf* indicates that this is something outwardly showy that vanishes upon examination, He indicated this by saying, emphasizing what is established in people's minds, that the noble ones are in such matters, and what was established among them, that the happy one in this world is happy in the Hereafter, assuming it exists: ﴿وإنْ﴾, meaning, and ﴿كُلُّ ذَلِكَ﴾, meaning, this matter, which is far from goodness because it is for the most part removed from what pleases Us. Also, its possessor remains poor even if the world gathers for him both dominion and kingship, because something will always remain in his soul that his power cannot reach, so he is always deprived. ﴿لَمّا﴾, meaning, except. This is according to the reading of ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah with the doubled *mim*. In the reading of the rest, with the single *mim*, it distinguishes the negative *lā* from the lightened *in*. *Mā* is emphatic, and the predicate is ﴿مَتاعُ الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾, meaning, the enjoyment of the worldly life, whose name indicates its lowliness, and that it has a rival, which is the Hereafter. It ends with death. Therefore His mercy required that He not restrict the believers in most cases, because abundance would diminish them in the Hereafter and the reckoning would be prolonged. ﴿والآخِرَةُ﴾, meaning, the Hereafter, to which no abode is equal, rather it is the true abode, indeed it is. (p-427)

Since attributing something to the Majestic indicates the majesty of the one attributed to, He said ﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ﴾, and by describing Him as Lord He indicated that majesty is with goodness and comfort, and by attributing it to Him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace (ﷺ), it reaches the highest ends: ﴿لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾, meaning, those who are always pausing before even the slightest act of disposal unless there is evidence, and no one else shares it with them. This is when ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) mentioned Kisra and Qaysar and the blessings they had, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Are you not content that they have this world and we have the Hereafter?" It is not far-fetched that what the sinners among the tyrants came to possess, such as the ornamenting of buildings, the construction of ceilings, and other evils of trials, could be a sign that people will become one community in disbelief near the Hour, so that the Hour will not come upon anyone who says "Allah." In the time of the Dajjal (the Deceiver), those who remain upon the truth will be extremely few, such that they will not be counted against the disbelievers, because the speech of kings is never free of reality, even if it comes out in the form of a condition. So how about the King of kings?

[p. 428] Since the intended meaning is: "But We did not make that a sign from Us that people were about to become one community, though We do oppose whoever We have created inclined toward good, toward faith. Yet what he is given in this world diminishes his standing in the Hereafter, because whoever is granted abundance in his worldly life, for the most part, becomes preoccupied and turns away from the remembrance of Allah. The angels then recoil from him, and the devils cling to him, and this drives him toward every evil. But whoever fears Allah and constantly remembers Him is strengthened by an angel, who becomes his helper." He then connects to this His saying, expressing the heedlessness of insight through *al-'ashā* (dimness of sight), which is weakness of vision, to depict those who forget the remembrance of Allah in the most repulsive form, as a warning against that: ﴿And whoever turns blind﴾, meaning, acts in the manner of the blind, whether his sight is dimmed by night and day or he is blind, according to an irregular reading transmitted from Ya'qub with a *fatḥa* on the *shīn*, and he sets affairs in disorder, going beyond ﴿the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾, whose mercy encompasses all things, so that no one receives mercy except that it comes from Him. This is as these people did when We gave them enjoyment, they and their fathers, and that made them insolent, though it was a very small thing. So they turned away from the signs and proofs and looked at them only with a weak glance, like the glance of one whose sight has been dimmed. ﴿We appoint﴾, meaning, We establish, empower, and decree a punishment ﴿for him﴾ for his turning away from the remembrance of Allah, ﴿a devil﴾, meaning, a fiery being far from mercy, who is dominant, encompassing him and constricting him, like the *qayḍ* of an egg, which is the inner membrane. ﴿He becomes his close companion﴾, bound to him as a captive is bound, constantly attached, so he cannot free himself from him as long as he remains blind to the remembrance of Allah. He is made to see blindness as fine and is led to think he is on the path of guidance. Just as whoever seeks insight through the remembrance of the Most Merciful has an angel subjected to him who becomes his friend and gives him good news of every good. Thus the remembrance of Allah is a strong fortress against the devil; whenever the servant leaves it, the enemy takes him captive, as has been reported in the hadith. [p. 429] Al-Qamus says: *al-ʿashā* with a short vowel is poor sight by night and day, or blindness, *ʿashiya* like *riḍiya* and *daʿā*. *Al-ʿashwa*, with a *ḍamma* or *kasra*, is embarking on a matter without clear understanding. Ibn Jarir said: The root of *al-ʿashw* is looking without firmness due to a defect in the eye. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': The root of the language is that the letters *ʿayn*, *shīn*, and the weak letter indicate darkness, scarcity, and lack of clarity in a thing.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 37:

Since "min" (from among) is general, and the qarin (companion, the devil who accompanies a person) is a collective noun, and He used the singular because He specified each individual, the sense is: "They indeed drive them toward kinds of baseness, open for them the doors of vices and afflictions, and make the committing of ugly deeds and calamities seem good to them." After this, He joined to it His saying, emphasizing what is in the hearts of the majority (as He indicated at the end of the verse) that the one who is given abundance is the one who is guided. This also indicates the abundance of those who go astray: ﴿And indeed they﴾, that is, the companions, ﴿hinder them﴾, that is, the ones who turn away (from the remembrance), ﴿from the way﴾, that is, the path whoever strays from it is ruined, because in reality there is no path other than it.

Since veering away from the way leads not to another way but to ruin, where no guide can show the right direction, it is a marvel. He followed it with another marvel, saying: ﴿And they think﴾, that is, the ones who turn away, despite their journeying into ruin because of the companions' adornment of desires and pleasures and their distancing of admonitions, ﴿that they are guided﴾, that is, that they are rooted in this description, because of the ease that is extended to them and the constriction that is placed upon those who remember.

[p. 430] Since the one who has strayed from the path, and the one who thinks he is upon the right course, does not persist for long, but his condition becomes clear to him soon, [the verse] adds a third wonder to the two preceding wonders as an explanation of it. Its implied meaning is: "We give this heedless one respite as a means of drawing him on, and as a trial for others, and We extend that over the length of his life," ﴿until﴾. He confirmed the report with His saying ﴿when﴾. Since he knew from the plural form in what was said that the intended meaning is the genus, and since the singular is the strongest indication of encompassing each individual, the expression in the singular was more frightening. Since the context indicated who the pronoun refers to, He said ﴿he comes to Us﴾, meaning the heedless one. Whoever reads it in the dual intends the heedless one and his companion. ﴿He says﴾, meaning the heedless one, in remorse and regret, with no benefit to him from it, because the place of benefit has passed, and that place is the abode of action: ﴿"Would that between me and you, O companion," be ﴿the distance of the two easts﴾, meaning the distance between the east and the west, by way of taghlib (the figure of speech in which one of two paired terms is used to cover both; Arabic: taghlib), as said by Ibn Jarir and others; or the east of winter and the east of summer, meaning the distance of one from the other. Then he gave as the cause of this wish His saying, comprising all kinds of blameworthiness: ﴿"how evil a companion!"﴾, meaning: "Indeed I have come to know that you are the one who led me astray and brought me to this straitened life and this slippery place. And at this moment I have felt that the harm you used to inflict upon me is a grievous harm, [p. 431] so I was like one who scratches his body because of festering sores, until blood flows from it; at first he finds pleasure in it, while in itself it is extremely painful to him."

Since pain may afflict the body, and the implied sense, as the context indicates, is definite, it is said to them: "Today, that will not benefit you, the day you came to Us, when you wished for this wish, when you witnessed those terrors, your being partners today in the day of this world in wrongdoing, your collusion in it, and the mutual enmity among you," so He joins to it His saying: ﴿And it will not benefit you today﴾, that is, in the world, anything of benefit at all, ﴿since﴾ at the time when ﴿you wronged﴾, while you were partners in wrongdoing, cooperating in it and supporting one another in it. And each one of you says to his companion, out of delight in him, drawing near to him, and showing affection: "O would that we never part, for you are an excellent companion!" Then it is said to them, as a rebuke: ﴿That you, in the punishment﴾, that is, the great punishment, and He placed it first out of concern for deterring and warning against it, ﴿are partners﴾ (p-432), that is, your partnership in it is constant, your wronging yourselves with an inner wronging, through matters that nature has concealed upon the hearts, and this necessitates entanglement in the snares of sins that lead to the manifest punishment, on the day of wishing and on the Day of Resurrection, a manifest, perceptible punishment. This is like one who inflicts a deep wound while he is unconscious: he is certainly being tormented by it, but he feels it only when he wakes up. It is like your saying to people who intend to collude in killing a forbidden soul: "It will not benefit you today, since you cooperate in killing him, your partnership tomorrow in destruction through the narrow prison, the destructive beating, and the striking of necks." Your purpose in this is to deter them from their wrongdoing by reminding them that they will come to this state, and what they are in of mutual support will vanish, so nothing of it will benefit them. And God is the Granter of success. Thus the verse contains ihtibak (concealment through complementary omission), and by this there disappears from it what the grammarians' parsing had made a cause of confusion. "Fa-ya layta" to the end indicates the opposite of its implied counterpart in the second place, and "wa-lan yanfa'akum" to the end indicates its like in the first place.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 40:

When the Prophet (ﷺ) was extremely eager for them to turn towards faith, almost killing himself with grief over their turning away, and this admonition is such that no one with even the least intellect hears it without his heart being pierced, he turned back from his error and returned to his right guidance, [God] had recited to them [this], but they did not benefit from it. So it was as if it were said: these people are deaf and blind, surrounded by misguidance on every side, encompassing them in such a way that they can hardly be free of it. Thus there is no way for anyone to make them hear, nor to make them see, nor to guide them. He said, building upon this and making it a consequence of it, as a lightening of the burden on the Prophet (ﷺ) in what he suffers of distress in exerting himself to convey [the message] to them, out of eagerness for their turning towards [faith] and grief at their aversion, using the interrogative hamzah which indicates the negation of what the verse is meant to convey: ﴿Can you then﴾, that is, by yourself, without the will of God the Exalted, ﴿make the deaf hear﴾, when We have made them deaf by what We have poured into the ears of their understanding of the lead of wretchedness, ﴿or guide the blind﴾ whom We have blinded by what We have covered the sight of their insight with, of veils of stupidity and perdition. Thus what they chose for themselves of blindness became joined with their deafness. ﴿And whoever is﴾, that is, by nature and disposition, ﴿in clear error﴾, that is, clear in himself that he is astray and that he is encompassed by error, manifesting that to everyone, such that it is not hidden from anyone. So the meaning is: none of that is up to you; rather it rests with God, who is capable of everything. As for you, there is nothing upon you but conveying [the message].

(p-434) Since this was like one who despairs of them, and since despair of the opponent's reform necessarily leads to wishing for relief from him through the death of one of the two, [Allah] connected to the two suppositions His saying, making clear that the granting of respite to them is neither from incapacity regarding them nor from breaking the promise, and emphasizing it with the nun of emphasis, "mā" and then "anā," and the nominal sentence, for those who suppose otherwise. It is also because He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is honored in His sight, exalted (Glorified and Exalted is He) in His presence, so that taking him away would be unlikely, and it is his right that this be denied. Likewise, showing him what He has threatened them with, because it is presumed that honoring them is for his sake: ﴿So whether We take you away﴾, i.e., from among them, by death or otherwise, ﴿then indeed We will take vengeance upon them﴾, i.e., those whom the allusion mentioned earlier described as deaf, blind, and astray, because their senses will not benefit them, ﴿upon them﴾, i.e., after your departure, because your presence among them is the cause of delaying the punishment from them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 42:

﴿Whether We show you﴾ while you are among them, ﴿that which We have promised them﴾, i.e., of the punishment. He expressed it with "promise" (wa'd) so that it would indicate good by its wording and evil by its style, thus encompassing both. ﴿Then indeed We﴾, with what you know of Our greatness, of which you are the most knowing of creation regarding them, ﴿are over them omnipotent﴾, over both of these measures. He emphasized it with "inna" (indeed) because their actions are the actions of one who denies His power. Likewise [He emphasized it] by using the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama) and the form of ifti'al (ita'ahum/iqtidar form). One of these two measures has been preceded by the eternal knowledge that it will not occur. So the verse is among the proofs of God's power to do the impossible for others, and these are very numerous. God has honored our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) by not showing him anything he would dislike regarding his community, until he passed away.

Since Allah (glorified and exalted be He) had left the listener suspended between fear and hope with these two conditional clauses, to demonstrate that knowledge of the Unseen belongs to Him alone, giving precedence to fear, and since the context, although conditional, conveyed that retribution against them is something that must occur, and that no one has the power to harm them or benefit them except Allah, He followed this with His saying: ﴿So hold fast﴾, meaning: seek and establish, with great earnestness, steadfast adherence in every state ﴿to what has been revealed to you﴾ from the time of your prophethood until now, both in regard to retribution against them and in everything else.

Since the situation, given the great number of opponents, required emphasis that would comfort the hearts of the followers and motivate them toward good adherence, He gave the reason for this with His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are upon a path﴾, meaning a broad, very clear road ﴿that is straight﴾, one that leads to the intended goal, into which no deviation can possibly enter at all. So when you do this, no harm from their vengeance will reach you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 44:

When he had established its excellence in itself, which requires that it be adhered to, he joined to it its benefit for them (p-436). And, to counter their denial, he said: ﴿And indeed it﴾, that is, the one revealed to you in this world, ﴿is indeed a reminder﴾, that is, a very great honour, an admonition and an exposition. He expressed the honour by the word "reminder" to draw attention to the fact that its cause is devotion to the Reminder, to what it has explained and prescribed, holding firmly to it, and attending to its matter. ﴿For you and for your people﴾: Quraysh in particular, the Arabs in general, and all who follow you, even if others are not of them, by virtue of its being revealed to one of them and in their tongue, so that all other people become followers of them; and by virtue of its bequeathing the good way and the pure, wide sciences, and its effect of making them dominant over all groups and of leadership for Quraysh in particular, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This affair will remain in Quraysh so long as two people remain among mankind who establish the religion." Whoever establishes this religion will be honoured and mentioned in the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Ibn al-Jawzi said: al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that "when the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked, 'To whom will this affair belong after you?', he did not inform them of anything until this verse was revealed, and after that, whenever he was asked, he said: 'To Quraysh.'" This indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ) understood from this that he would govern the Muslims by the authority of prophethood and the honour of the Qur'an, and that his people would succeed him in governance by the honour of the Qur'an which was revealed to a man (p-437) of them. End of quotation.

When the implication was: "You will then be exalted above all kings and you will know," he joined to it His saying: ﴿And you will be questioned﴾, that is, you will become, in all kinds of knowledge, the place to which the seekers of religion and worldly matters make their journeys, such that all the people of the earth, from the People of the Book and others, will question you about what concerns them of the matters of their religion and their worldly affairs, because they believe that no one will equal you in knowledge, after you were, in their eyes, the most contemptible of nations in weakness and ignorance, as happened to the Children of Israel when Allah raised them up. That was the furthest thing from Pharaoh and his household, and for this reason they used to mock those signs laughingly, and attributed to the one who brought them what does not befit his lofty station of impossibilities. And you will be questioned about His right, the discharge of His thanks, and how you were in acting upon it and responding to it. This is a true promise in which there is no failure at all.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 45:

When He, glory be to Him, had refuted the divinity of other than Him, which ignorance had led to, and continued until He concluded with knowledge that necessitates knowing the truth, the implied meaning was a refutation of their illusory doubt, which says ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 20]. So He summoned all that was revealed to you, and contemplate it with the utmost contemplation: do you see in it any obscurity regarding divinity for anything besides Allah? He then joined to it his words, negating a scriptural proof, as was indicated by His words ﴿Or have We given them a Book﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 21], ﴿and ask those whom We sent﴾, that is, according to our greatness. Since what can be known of them from the traces of the Messengers is only for Musa and Isa and those prophets of the Children of Israel who came between them, peace be upon them, who preserve their sunnah from the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Book of the Prophets, He said, affirming the preposition that conveys a certain time: ﴿from before you﴾.

Since their followers had altered and changed, so that there was no trust in them, He expressed it with "the Messengers" and said: ﴿from Our messengers﴾, that is, by the reading of their followers of their books, some of which they had distorted. And you made your Book a guardian over them, for when they recite them in your presence and present them to you, you will know their meanings, expose their distortion, and show the agreement of all the books by returning what was confused for them from their mutashabih (ambiguous verses) to their muhkam (clear verses). So the meaning of this is close to the meaning of the verse of Yunus, ﴿So ask those who read the Book before you﴾ [Yunus: 94], and of the verse of al-Anbiya, ﴿This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 24], with added indication of their distortion. So what is truly asked is the inimitable Qur'an upon the tongue of the Messenger, to whom all the Messengers bore witness, those from whom the covenant was taken to believe in him and follow him. By this explanation the weakness of the view of one who said that the meaning is the actual asking of the Messengers, those who were gathered for him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) on the night of al-Isra' (the Night Journey), becomes clear. The purpose of this is nothing but the rebuke of the disbelievers from among the Arabs, and of those from the People of the Book who were powerful over them, by their saying: "Your religion is better than his, and you are more rightly guided in the way than he is." When they bring their books, you will know their decisive indication of His exclusive right to worship, as I have explained in this book of mine, and it returns the ambiguous among them to the clear.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) considered it similar to His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿If you disagree about anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [An-Nisa': 59]. He said: "It is known that the meaning of that is: refer it to the Book of Allah and the sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace." He said: "So [the verse] dispensed with mentioning the books by mentioning the Messengers." This is exactly what I have said. Had the intended meaning been the literal asking, and the asking of all the Messengers, He would have said "qablaka" (before you) with "man" dropped, so that it would encompass all. And Allah knows best.

When He mentioned the one being asked, magnifying him through what the phrasing required of sending and of attribution to Him, He mentioned the one being asked about by His words, the Exalted: ﴿Have We appointed﴾, that is, permitted, commanded and approved, according to our greatness and complete power, of what contradicts that, and He established the worthlessness of what is other than Him by His words: ﴿besides the Most Merciful﴾, and He added by His words: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾, that is, the One whose mercy encompasses all existing things, ﴿gods﴾. Since a god had been made for each people, and a direction to which they turn in their worship, and a tangible object, owing to the dominance of imaginings over understandings, which they witness, and since perhaps someone who is obstinate might dispute it, He said, guarding against this: ﴿to be worshipped﴾, that is, from a worshipper in some way.

Since the affluent are inclined to despise whoever brings them a refutation of their corrupt aims with some kind of contempt, as the disbelievers of Quraysh said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 31], and they continue to repel this and similar errors until the Possessor of Majesty overpowers them with what His messengers brought them, either by destroying them or otherwise, even if they were at the height of strength, He, glory be to Him, cited the story of Musa, peace be upon him, as a witness to that, with what Pharaoh said to Musa, peace be upon him, of a similar kind, and of His destroying him despite his strength, and of His rescuing the Children of Israel despite their weakness, and as consolation and hope for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Since the intended meaning is: "We indeed sent all of Our messengers, and they were the most noble of creation, with the tawhid (monotheism; the affirmation of God's oneness) that you have come with. In sending them, We did not take into account what the nations desired of status, wealth, or anything else. So there is no ground for relying on you in what We sent you with, of tawhid and other matters, nor for opposing you in it." He then linked to it the first of those who guided people to asking the followers of the messengers, saying, emphasizing the most important thing with which they contend, namely the denial of prophethood. He used the particle of expectation (ḥarf al-tawaqquʿ) because of what it implies of the command to ask the messengers, peace and blessings be upon them: ﴿Indeed, We sent﴾, meaning, with what manifested of Our greatness.

Since the sending from Him, glory be to Him, is not according to the standard of greatness in this world as its people see it, as these said, ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down...﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31] and so on, He said, contradicting them: ﴿Moses﴾, that is, the one whom Pharaoh thought most deserving of his honor, because he had raised and nurtured him, ﴿with Our signs﴾, that is, those with which he overpowered the great ones of creation and their tyrants. This indicates the truth of his claim and of all the signs, since they are equal in power and in breaking custom. Since the context concerns the Prophet (ﷺ) asking the messengers about the matter of tawhid, the signs were sufficient, so authority (sulṭān) was not mentioned, because it pertains to subjugation and domination: ﴿to Pharaoh﴾, that is, because he transgressed, oppressed, and claimed that he was the Supreme Lord, and the misguided agreed with him, ﴿and his chiefs﴾ [Yunus: 88], those whom he made into gods besides Him and whom his people worshipped; so he did not leave them in that, because We were not pleased with it. ﴿He said﴾ because of Our sending him, ﴿Indeed, I am a messenger﴾, and he emphasized it because of their denial of what your people denied of prophethood. Since kindness is a cause of submission, he said: ﴿of the Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, their Owner, their Nurturer, and their Manager.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 47:

Since they had done, in rejecting His messenger (ﷺ) and mocking his message, what Quraysh had done, He said, consoling the Prophet (ﷺ) and threatening them, as a causal explanation of what its implied sense is: "They said to him: Bring a sign." So he brought it, in the manner already mentioned more than once, with clarity and beauty like the sun: ﴿So when he brought them Our signs﴾ by bringing the two signs of the hand and the staff, in which they witnessed Our greatness and which indicated to them Our power over all the signs, ﴿behold, they laughed at them﴾, that is, all of them, mocking Our messenger, while he and those who believed in his message and in what he brought from Us had long been laughing at them on the Day of Regret and Remorse. ﴿They laughed at them﴾, that is, they hastened to laugh at the coming of the signs without pause or reluctance, with derision and mockery.

al-Biqa'i said: Since someone might suppose that the signs admit some of that (that they can be lessened or diminished), Allah, glory be to Him, described their condition with His words: ﴿And We do not show them﴾, meaning, and the situation is that We do not show them, with the majesty, exaltedness, and perfection that are Ours, and He intensified the negation by affixing the preposition (al-jarr, the prepositional particle ب/min) and the exclusive particle (adat al-hasr, the particle of restriction), for the sake of those who might imagine that they are excused in their laughing. So He said: ﴿any sign except that it is greater﴾, meaning in rank, ﴿than its sister﴾, meaning the one that preceded it, in relation to the knowledge of those who look at it. This is because the human being, due to his forgetfulness, when the second of two equal things comes to him, sees all that came to him as forgotten and not some of what came first, so he is certain that it is greater than it. Or this is a kinaya (metonymy) for the fact that all of them are at the utmost of greatness, as their poet said:

"Whomever you meet among them, you say, 'I have met their chief.'"

Or the greatness between them is general and specific from one aspect. The better of these views is what Ibn Jarir indicated: that every sign is clearer in proof against them and more emphatic than what preceded it, because it indicates what the earlier one indicated and adds the strength that the reinforcement gives in magnitude. Thus it becomes, together with what preceded it, greater than what preceded it when it arrives and the proof is established by it.

Since the implied sense is: they persisted in their disbelief and did not return to any of the signs, because We had made them deaf and blind and encompassed them with misguidance, given Our knowledge of their state, He followed it with His words: ﴿And We seized them﴾, meaning a seizing of subjugation and dominance, ﴿with punishment﴾, meaning all of it, because We made its blows successive upon them in a manner informing that We are capable of whatever We will from it. So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood, ﴿as distinct signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 133]. And al-qitaʿ (the hail/plagues) is large hail, the like of which was not known, blazing with fire, and the death of the firstborn. These were signs of the truthfulness of Musa, upon him be peace, by what they had of miraculous inimitability, and a punishment for them in this world joined to the punishment of the Hereafter. How wondrous is such overwhelming power and manifest wisdom! ﴿so that they might return﴾, meaning so that their state, in the eyes of the observer who is ignorant of the outcomes, would be the state of one whose return is hoped for.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 49:

When Pharaoh was subjected, in many of the plagues with which He (glorified is He) struck him, as has passed in al-A'raf citing the Torah, he would say to Musa (peace be upon him): "You have erred, and the Lord is righteous, while I and my people are wicked. So pray before the Lord, for He is One of forbearance and patience, and He will turn this away from me." Then, when God removed that from them, they would return to the wickedness they had been upon. Their act of this kind was the act of one who does not believe that Musa (peace be upon him) is truly a prophet, but rather believes that he is a sorcerer and that his deeds are merely imagination. Thus He expressed this meaning by His saying, coordinated with what is implied in "but they did not turn back": ﴿And they said﴾, that is, Pharaoh directly and his followers in agreement with him: ﴿O sorcerer﴾. They addressed him with the particle of distance, together with the implication conveyed by "they said" rather than "they called out", that he is present, indicating his distance from their hearts. The expression of this is a rebuke to the Quraysh, by way of indicating that they and others who passed before them hurl the accusation of sorcery at the Messenger, and yet acknowledge his message when they need his supplication to remove what their Lord has punished them with. That is incompatible with what they claim of steadfastness, courage, intellect, fairness and nobility. This is what happened to the Quraysh when "the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O God, help me against them with years like the years of Joseph.' So they suffered famine. When the calamity grew severe upon them, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb came to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the noble city of Medina and said: 'O Muhammad! You have come with the bond of kinship, and your people have perished, so pray to God for them.' He prayed for them and they were relieved." Without doubt, the reality of their condition, which God has mentioned, is a contradiction that no rational person would accept for himself: describing him as a sorcerer, while asking him for supplication. Belief that he is a sorcerer prevents requesting his supplication, and belief that he is a sorcerer prevents, for the rational person, asking him for supplication. ﴿Pray for us to your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you by what He does with you of these acts which you forbade us, honoring you ﴿by what﴾, that is, by virtue of what ﴿He has covenanted with you﴾, that He does of removing and lifting according to what you wish, as you informed us that if we believe, He honors us, and if we persist, He humiliates us. Then they gave the reason for that by their saying, emphatically, bringing near their far-off state from transgression by what the witness of existence reports: ﴿Indeed, we are guided﴾, that is, guidance that is established, becoming for us an enduring attribute when that is removed from us.

Since a sensible person does not report about himself except what is true, how much more so when he is great among his people, and how much more so when he confirms that with various kinds of emphasis, so that the listener of this speech would be certain of its truth, Allah the Exalted clarified what confirms that their condition is that of one who believes him to be a sorcerer, in that they hastened to betray with lies in it without shame or fear. So He said, expressing it with the particle "fa" (then) as an indication of that: ﴿So when We removed from them the punishment﴾, upon what We possess of greatness that terrifies the mountains, ﴿the punishment﴾, i.e., which We had sent down upon them, ﴿behold, they broke their word﴾, i.e., they met the removal (of the punishment) by renewing the breaking (of their promise), with one breach after another.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 51:

﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾, meaning, in addition to his breaking of his covenant. ﴿Among his people﴾, meaning those who were most fully committed to standing with him. He ordered each of them to spread his words widely, in a way that reaches the distant as well as the near, so that it would be like a public proclamation, informing them that he remained steadfast in disbelief, lest some of them suppose that he had turned back. Since it was as if it had been said, "Why did he proclaim?", he answered with his words: ﴿He said﴾, meaning, out of fear of the conversion of the Qibt (the Egyptians/Copts), because he saw that the manifest signs they had witnessed were of a kind that shakes and seizes hearts: ﴿O my people﴾, seeking their sympathy by informing them that they were one flesh, and urging them on by describing them as people of strength in what they attempt, establishing for them his excuse for his breaking of the covenant through his words: ﴿Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?﴾, meaning mine alone, ﴿all of it﴾, so that no one among the Children of Israel or others could object. The purpose was that this would yield, according to his claim, that his domination over the Children of Israel and his forcible removal of them from under his hand was a transgression against the one who truly holds sovereignty, and therefore would be corruption, so there is no harm upon him in deceiving those who did this to him, by means of what he had covenanted with them when the harm touched him. He did not read it with ṣarf (the tanwin, or nunation, which marks declension as an indeclinable proper noun is not given), so that it would be an explicit indication of his intended meaning of it being a proper name, and because the word miṣr is also applied to a single city, whereas tanwin comes for diminution, which is the opposite of his intention.

Since there had come to him, from what he had seen of the signs, and had befallen him from those blows with various kinds of punishments, what had bewildered him to the point that he came to be counted among those whose followers doubt his sovereignty, he indicated this by the state he created: ﴿And these﴾, meaning and the situation being that these ﴿rivers﴾, as though he had been greatly multiplying the cutting of canals to his gardens and palaces and similar matters, so he said: ﴿flow beneath me﴾, meaning from whatever place you wish, by means that no one but me can achieve. He increased the affirmation with his words: ﴿Do you not then see?﴾, meaning what I have mentioned to you, so that by the insight of your hearts you may know that it is not fitting for anyone to contend with me. By my life, this is the speech of one whose strength has weakened and whose bonds have come undone.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 52:

When the context guided us to the understanding that the implied meaning is: "Is this one who has come, who would strip us of our power over the Children of Israel, better in your eyes than I?", he linked to it his saying: ﴿Or am I better﴾, together with what I have described to you of my greatness, and of my power to cause the waters to flow, by which every living thing has life. Ibn al-Jawzi and other exegetes related from Sibawayh and his teacher al-Khalil that this is a counterpart (mu'adalah) to their being made to see (taqrir bil-ibsar). It is as if he said: "Will you not look at what I have reminded you of, so that you see, since you do not see, that he is better than me, or that I am better than him, because you do not see?" He was more deserving of this advice than they were, for he showed them the clear path to misguidance and what leads to it without any hardship or fatigue, by his saying: ﴿Will you not see? Or are you not seeing people?﴾ This constitutes ihtibak (interlocking ellipsis), whose intended sense is: "Will you not see what I have alerted you to?" He mentioned seeing first as evidence for the omission of its like second, and betterness second as evidence for the omission of its like first. He belittled, from the greatness of the one who came to him with those signs (ﷺ), so that people would not hasten to follow him, because his signs, being from Allah, are like the sun in radiance, loftiness and fame. So he said: ﴿from this﴾, using the demonstrative of nearness to express contempt for him. Then he described him with what makes his intent clear, saying: ﴿who is contemptible﴾, that is, weak, lowly, insignificant and humiliated, because he handles his affairs himself, and has no kingdom or power by which he causes a river to flow or executes a command. ﴿And hardly can he express himself clearly﴾, that is, he is not close to explaining any meaning, because of the speech impediment (habsah) in his tongue. So he is neither capable in himself nor has he any power through his tongue to turn meanings about and vary expression so as to draw hearts and astonish minds, so that his followers multiply and his affair grows great. In all of this he lied, for Musa, peace be upon him, was the most eloquent of his people's time in speech and deed, by Allah's decree, who sent him and commanded him. But the wicked one attributed this to what remained in his tongue of impediment, to make his followers imagine it, because Musa, peace be upon him, did not pray for the removal of his impediment, but only for a knot to be loosened from it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 53:

When Pharaoh and those like him, whose insight was obliterated and whose understanding was lacking, stood by the illusion that nearness to kings and dominion over affairs come only through abundance of worldly goods and adorning oneself with the ornaments of kings, he (Pharaoh) made his claim to a messengership from the King of kings, which necessarily entails nearness to Him, the basis of his saying: ﴿Why then have bracelets of gold been cast upon him?﴾ And since honours, gifts and robes of honour are bestowed upon the one who is honoured with them, he expressed it with that word, saying: ﴿been cast﴾, i.e., from whatever caster it might be, ﴿upon him﴾, from the presence of the one who sent him, who claims that he is the king in truth, ﴿bracelets﴾, plural of ﴿aswira﴾ (said by al-Zajjaj), and it is declined because it takes the form of a singular, like ʿalaniyya and karahiyya. The suwar is what is placed on the wrist of ornaments, ﴿of gold﴾, so that this would be a sign of the truth of the soundness of his claim, just as we do when we bestow upon one of our servants the sending to some region for one of the great matters, ﴿or the angels came with him﴾, i.e., accompanying him when he came to us with this momentous news and great tidings, ﴿the angels﴾, i.e., this kind, and he indicated their multitude by what he clarified of the state through his saying: ﴿arrayed together﴾, i.e., some of them accompany others, such that they fill the expanse and are in the utmost nearness to him, such that they accompany him so that this matter for which he came seeking might be granted, just as we do when we send a messenger to a matter requiring defence, dispute and contention. So the outcome of his affair, as you see, was that he was strengthened by the flowing of rivers, and God destroyed him by them, as an indication that whoever relies on anything apart from God, God destroys him by it. He belittled Moses, peace be upon him, and disparaged him for poverty and error, so He empowered him, as an indication that no one belittles anything without being overcome by it. — related by al-Qushayri.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 54:

When his speech was such that, to whoever reflects, it lowers him rather than raising him, and he had gone along with his followers, for they, with the expectation of gain without the favor, are the most abject of things to one for whom worldly leadership is established, even if it becomes dust, and the most disobedient of things to one whom people do not understand, even if he performs great feats, the listener yearned for what resulted from it, so he said: ﴿So he made light of his people﴾, that is, because of these deceptions with which he had enchanted them in this speech, which in reality belittles him, weakens his affair, and breaks his kingdom in the eyes of whoever has intellect, ﴿his people﴾, who have great strength. So he carried them, by his delusion, to what they were already prepared for in lightness of judgment, ﴿and they obeyed him﴾, by acknowledging his kingship, submitting to his grandeur, confessing his lordship, and rejecting the command of Musa, peace be upon him.

When his speech, as has passed, was the greatest weakening of his affair, and it is refuted (p-451) by the measure of its firmness, in that Musa, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, our Prophet and he, came with what dispenses with what he said about the bracelets and the appearance of the angels, in that whatever he threatened them with, whatever they asked of him, he answered them with it, there was no reason for the Copts to obey Pharaoh after they had seen the signs except conformity in the wickedness of souls. Allah, glory be to Him, explained this by His saying, emphasizing what suits their conditions, so that He approves their deeds, and they are the majority: ﴿Indeed they were﴾, that is, by what was in their natures of evil and hypocrisy, because they were ﴿a people﴾, that is, among them is a strength of restraints that makes them obstinate except before one who subdues them with the means of the world to which they are accustomed, ﴿defiantly disobedient﴾, that is, deeply immersed in going out from obedience to Allah into disobedience, such that this has become for them a second nature.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 55:

It seems that the period during which Moses (peace be upon him) tried to reason with them was short, and therefore He used the particle fa (then, immediately) in His words: ﴿So when they angered Us﴾, meaning they did, in its sense, what provokes anger with intense provocation, by provoking Our friends, as in the sacred hadith, "I was ill and you did not visit Me," because of their breaking their covenant again and again, one repetition after another, ﴿We took vengeance upon them﴾, meaning We inflicted upon them, by way of requital for what they did to Our Messenger (peace be upon him), a great, abhorrent, detestable punishment, (p-452) as if by a single effort, ﴿so We drowned them﴾ in the sea, ﴿all of them﴾, the destruction of a single soul, so that not one of them escaped, despite their large numbers, their strength and their severity. This does not usually happen except after great effort or great attention.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 56:

Since their destruction came about because they angered God and were arrogant toward His messengers, they became a cause for those who came after them to take warning from their condition. Therefore God the Exalted said: ﴿So We made them﴾, meaning: by Our seizing them in this manner, through drowning and other means that preceded it, ﴿a precedent﴾, going before everyone who would be destroyed after them, a destruction of wrath, in perdition in this world and punishment in the Hereafter, ﴿and an example﴾ for whoever desires to exalt himself on earth, so that his end will be perdition in both abodes or in one of them, the same as their end. As He, glorified and exalted is He, the Lord of all creatures, said: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [28:41]. ﴿And a parable﴾, meaning a wondrous report that travels like a proverb (mathal), ﴿for the later ones﴾, those who came after them from their time until the end of time. Their condition thus becomes a lesson for some people and a misguidance for others. Whoever has decreed for himself to be in the likeness of their condition acts like their deeds, and whoever wishes to be saved from what befell them avoids their actions. Whoever God wills good for is granted the success of a good example that turns him back from his error, and whoever God wills evil for is given from among them an example by which he emboldens himself in his evil and strengthens himself in his wickedness and deceit. The wicked one makes what they were given of this world, of blessing, luxurious comfort, prosperity and victory, an example for himself in attaining by it what they had from injustice. He makes their destruction an example of what is to be avoided, so that he keeps away from their deeds in order to escape the like of their punishment. One of them says: "Such-and-such people were seized with the seizing of the family of Pharaoh," meaning no one among them escaped, and similar sayings of their kind in all their circumstances. We say: "Indeed We destroy whoever wrongs and persists in his wrong after Our warning him, and who is overbearing, even if his family and followers are great and he thinks his might and his protection are secure, like the custom of the family of Pharaoh." The one who wishes evil says: "There is no one on the face of the earth who will remain if he fears the consequences," so he refrains from his desires, plunges into the gardens of his inclinations and his will, and savors the good things of life. Likewise, his own self, as happened to Pharaoh, for he did not turn back from anything of his dominion, nor from reaching the utmost limit of his arrogance and vanity, until he was taken away as others were taken, whether he followed his course or not. Indeed, a people went astray through him and led others astray, and they loosened for those who approached them the bonds of religion and so they slipped. And this was not enough for them, until they claimed that he was among the most honored of those brought near, because the last of his words was faith; so he severed what had been before it, and he was not defiled after it, and he died pure and purified, with nothing of the defilement in him. Yet this was only at the moment of despair, when there is no benefit in it. They also deceived the weak by saying: "There is no explicit statement in the Qur'an about his punishment after death," thereby blinding them to the decisive proof that is ordered by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the transgressors﴾ [10:83], and ﴿Indeed the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾ [40:43]. From this it follows, beyond any doubt, that Pharaoh is among the companions of the Fire. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and threw them into the sea. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾ [28:40], and ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [28:41].

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The people of Noah, and ʿĀd, and Pharaoh, the one of the stakes, denied before them﴾ [38:12], until He said: ﴿Each of them denied the messengers, so My punishment was justified﴾ [38:14], besides that from the clear verses and manifest proofs. Likewise, apart from Pharaoh and his people, God, glorified is He, made the righteous and the wicked a precedent and an example for the later ones. Whoever wills good for himself is made to follow a like good that he takes as a model, and whoever wills evil for himself is misled by a like evil that he follows. God made ʿĪsā (Jesus), peace be upon him, an example of the completeness of His power to originate things through means and without means. He was the most devout worshipper of his time, the most knowledgeable, the most ascetic, the nearest to good and the farthest from evil. Whoever God wills good for followed him in that and was guided by him, while others went astray through him and struck for themselves likenesses of gods, and they came to rejoice in what no intelligent person would approve or regard as right. Your people also struck him as an example for their gods when He told us that they, together with them, are fuel for Hell, and they were pleased by this, delighted, and they thought they had won and prevailed.

When the son of Mary was cited as an example, behold, your people raise a clamour at it.

Ibn Maryam (the son of Mary) — ḍuriba means that someone among them struck it, i.e., cited it, as a mathal (a parable or example) for their gods. Qawmuka (your people) means those to whom We gave the power to carry out what they attempt. Minhu (from it) means that example. Yaṣiddūn means they raise their voices and clamour loudly, out of joy that they had, in their own claim, triumphed through a contradiction; thus they turn away from answering your call. It is said: ṣadda ʿanhu ṣudūdan, meaning he turned away; and ṣadda yaṣuddu and yaṣillu means he clamoured. So said al-Qamus. Therefore Ibn al-Jawzi said: both meanings are the same — that is, the reading with a ḍamma on the ṣad and the reading with a kasra — they clamour. It is possible that the meaning of the ḍamma reading is: they turn away. Ibn Burjan said: the kasra is the higher of the two readings.

This is because the Quraysh said, as has passed in al-Anbiya', "Indeed we and what we worship are fuel for Hell." It necessarily follows that ʿIsa would be like that, and that we and our gods would be equal in regard to him, for he was worshipped, and we are content with his equality with us — to the end of what they said (p. 456). And what He, Glorified is He, answered them with, from the verse of general application which is intended to be specific, as is required by their speech and their tongue, namely that the original use of "mā" is for what does not reason. That is what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He, relating about them:

[Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 58]

﴿And they said: "Are our gods better, or he?"﴾ That is, the idols and angels that we worship are better, or Jesus? So we are content to be with him.

When the eagerness for their answer became intense, and the answer to this had already been given in [surah] al-Anbiya', he [al-Biqa'i] placed here the point that their intention in this was nothing but contentiousness (al-mumahakah), obstinacy (al-mumahalah), evasion (al-murawaghah), and combativeness (al-muqatalah). So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They did not strike this example for you except for the sake of disputation.﴾ That is, the unbelievers did not strike this example, Ibn al-Za'bara literally, and others among your people figuratively, comparing their gods to Jesus, upon him be peace. ﴿Except for the sake of disputation﴾ means, to intend that they might silence you from your call through sophistry (mughalatah), while they know that what they imposed upon you is not necessarily binding, and they never believed it to be binding. This is because the discussion was only about their idols, and because restriction (al-khusus) is common in their speech, and because He followed it with what specifies the restriction and removes the ambiguity, even on the assumption of conceding it. So they never accepted as binding what they were held to. ﴿Rather, they are a people﴾ meaning, people possessing strength to pursue by means of what they attempt, ﴿quarrelsome﴾ meaning, of fierce contention, capable of vehement obstinacy.

Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah narrated from (p-457) Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No people went astray after guidance that they had been upon except that they were given to disputation," then he recited the verse.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 59:

Since this has implied that he is not a mere object of contempt, he stated it explicitly in the form of restriction (qasr), a qasr qalb (restriction that corrects a false belief) directed at those who claim that he is exclusively divine. So He said: ﴿He was only a servant﴾, i.e., he, Jesus, peace be upon him, ﴿is only a servant﴾, and not a god, ﴿upon whom We bestowed favor﴾, i.e., through the greatness and beneficence that belong to Us, ﴿and We made him﴾, by means of the extraordinary breaches of custom We wrought in his birth and his other signs, ﴿an example﴾, i.e., a wondrous matter, clear and manifest, yet containing in it something obscure and a place of doubt, namely that We created him from a female alone, without the intermediary of a male, so that thereby He might lead astray whoever stops at what is sensed. We guided to the truth concerning him by the extraordinary signs We granted him, the purity of his character, the goodness of his disposition and the nobility of his lineage, as a felicity for whoever We raised, through the light of his heart and the purity of his intellect, to excellent contemplation of meanings. ﴿For the Children of Israel﴾, who are the people most knowing of him, some through direct witness and some through close transmission. When he came to them in that manifest state, being truly so by the miracles that occurred at his hands and at the hands of his mother, whoever God granted sight of the truth regarding his affair believed in him, through the miracles that were in him. Whenever one of them saw a man following his path in his deeds and his nobility, he was guided to the truth of his affair, and he would say: "This is his example, Jesus, peace be upon him," and he benefited by the Prophet and whoever followed him with excellence, and so attained God's good pleasure. He also said, this one who has been granted success, discerning the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him: "His example in this is the example of his father Adam, peace be upon him, in his being brought forth from a female without a male; rather, Adam, peace be upon him, is more wondrous. And like his maternal cousin Yahya, whom Zakariya and Ishaq, peace be upon them both, found in the bringing forth of each of them through a cause that is in the utmost weakness. These are his good examples." And whoever God intended to be led astray among them said other than that, of the impossible. So when they made for Him the worst of examples, God struck upon them humiliation and wretchedness. Ibn Burjan said: He singled them out for mention because they are the ones who are seduced by the Dajjal and who hasten toward him. Then he said: The example in this is only when the Dajjal comes with those signs, calling to himself, and opposes what Jesus, peace be upon him, brings of raising the dead and of being strengthened by the Holy Spirit; that is, he leads astray from the manifest matter whoever God intends to test. End of quotation. The better view is that the meaning of his being an example is that He made his affair so clear that he is cited as an example, thereby clarifying it for others, while he himself has no need of an example to clarify him for whoever possesses even a little insight.

Since the implied sense is: "If We willed, We would have made all of you from females without males, and if We willed, We would have made you equal to them in that humiliation which We imposed upon them when they attributed to Him the worst of likenesses; so We increased what you are in of humiliation and abasement beyond the rest of the nations, in that their dominion over you became such that they plundered you. And if We willed, We would have wiped you all out from the face of the earth and left it a house with no one to keep it company?" He followed this with His words: ﴿And if﴾, expressing it in the present tense, as an indication of the permanence of His power to renew creation, so He said: ﴿We willed, We would have made﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness, something more wondrous than what We did in the matter of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, ﴿from among you﴾, that is, a making that originates from you, either by generation, as We made ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, from a female without a male, and We made Ādam, peace be upon him, from dust without female or male; or by substitution, ﴿angels upon the earth, succeeding one another﴾, that is, they would be successors to you, one after another, after your annihilation, so We would make them an example for you, just as We made ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, an example for the Children of Israel. It is also possible that the meaning is: We would have made some of you angels by transforming their creation, so that We would make them successors to those who turned away from them, and some of them would succeed others; for they are among Our servants, bodies that accept generation just as they accept origination. On both interpretations, this is an indication that the angels are contingent beings among His servants, glorified is He, who direct them in His will as He wills, whether in the heavens or on the earth; nothing of you is at all far from the rank of divinity, as guidance for them toward the true belief concerning His glorified affair, by the comprehensiveness of His power and the perfection of His knowledge, the necessary implication of which is that there is no god but Him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 61:

When He, glorified be He, mentioned the (making of) annihilation and the succession that follows from it as a obligation, He mentioned that His sending him down to the earth at the end of time is a sign of the annihilation of people as a certainty, so He said, emphasizing it for the sake of their denial: ﴿And indeed he﴾, that is, Jesus, peace be upon him, ﴿is surely a sign of the Hour﴾, that is, his descent is a cause for knowledge of the nearness of the Hour, which is his annihilating all creatures by death. Likewise, what is related from him, that he would give life and heal the sick, is a great cause for certainty about the Hour, which is the Resurrection. So he is a cause for knowledge of both matters: the generality of annihilation and the generality of resurrection.

Since the Quraysh used to seek counsel from the Jews, asking them, because they were People of the Book, about the affair of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Christians were likewise in this, and since Jesus, peace be upon him, being one of the signs of the Hour was a matter definitively established by both groups, the Christians say that he is the one who came to them and was raised up to heaven, as is held by us, while the Jews say that he has not yet come and will come later. Thus the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him, was established in what Allah, exalted is He, related about His favor upon him, and that he is one of the signs of the Hour, by the testimony of the three groups, Jews, Christians and Muslims, with a very great certainty, so that it became as though it were witnessed directly. Therefore He made the statement that preceded, delivered through His Prophet, peace be upon him, turning the speech to address them directly and emphasizing it in response to their denial of it, on the basis of what was established by the testimony of the three groups: ﴿So do not be in doubt about it﴾, that is, do not harbor the slightest doubt, nor waver the slightest wavering, nor deny the slightest denial, nor dispute the slightest dispute, ﴿concerning it﴾, that is, because of it. It is said: "marā al-shay'" and "amtarāhu" meaning he extracted it; "marāhu mi'at sawt" meaning he struck him a hundred times; "marāhu ḥaqqahu" meaning he denied his right; and al-mirya, with a dammah or a kasrah, means disputation and doubt. ﴿And follow Me﴾, that is, make your following of Me your utmost effort. ﴿This﴾, that is, all that I have commanded you of this and other matters, ﴿is a path﴾, that is, a broad, clear road, ﴿straight﴾, that is, without any crookedness in it.

When he had urged them to follow the path of the Protecting Friend, the Praiseworthy, by the guidance of the Compassionate, sincere, Kind and Merciful One, he warned them against the distant enemy, the burnt and expelled one. He said, indicating the greatness of his temptation through his power to beautify desires, to seize from a place of safety, to confuse what is unclear, and to cover fear with emphasis, while they follow his opposite by way of imitation: ﴿And let not Satan avert you﴾, that is, from this clear, broad, straight path that leads to the goal with the least effort, ﴿Satan﴾. Since it was as though it were said (p-462), "What is wrong with him that he diverts us from the way of our Lord?", he mentioned the cause as a warning in His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is to you﴾, that is, all of you, and the statement was emphasized because the actions of those who follow you are the actions of one who denies his enmity: ﴿a clear enemy﴾, that is, evident in enmity in himself, proclaiming it. This is by his extremity in enmity toward your father, to the point that by his casting him down he brought you down from the place of rest to the place of toil. It is an enmity arising from envy, so it never ceases, ever.

When Allah, glory be to Him, had already stated that He bestowed favour upon ʿIsa, peace be upon him, and made him an example for the Children of Israel, and had hinted at their disagreement, and that some of them had fallen into the like of what he was (wrongly) upon, and had warned those who follow them into similar error, and had commanded following the guide and forbidden following the misleader, He then made explicit what their condition was when Allah brought him forth to them in that strange state. So He said, conjoining it to what was earlier estimated after His saying ﴿And We made him an example﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 59]: ﴿And when ʿIsa came﴾, that is, to the Children of Israel after Musa, upon both of them be peace: ﴿with clear proofs﴾, that is, with signs that are heard and seen,

﴿he said﴾, alerting them: ﴿Indeed I have come to you﴾ with what definitely shows you that it is a sign from Allah and also a word from Him, ﴿with wisdom﴾, that is, a matter that is firmly established, which cannot be undone and cannot be repelled except by obstinacy, so that I may clear you by it of the error into which you have fallen. (p-463) Since the intended meaning of "wisdom" was what had been abrogated of the Torah and other than it, of everything that had come to them with him, the implied sense was: that you follow him and abandon what you were upon. Then he specified a particular matter which is among the most firm of wisdom, saying: ﴿and to make clear to you﴾, that is, a very clear clarification, ﴿some of that about which you differ﴾, that is, now, ﴿concerning it﴾, and you continually renew disagreement because of it. This "some" is apparently, as the end of the verse indicates, the ambiguous matter (al-mutashabih) because of which they disbelieved; he clarified it with a clarification that returns it to the decisive matter (al-muhkam). It may also be that it is some of the ambiguous, namely that whose clarification suffices to return the rest of the ambiguous to the decisive by analogy with it. For the norm in every book is that it combines the decisive and the ambiguous. The decisive (al-muhkam) is that which has no confusion in it, and the ambiguous (al-mutashabih) is that which causes confusion, and within it is that which returns it to the decisive, but by way of symbol and allusion, which only the people of insight taste, so that thereby the truthful is distinguished from the liar. The truthful one, who has firmly rooted knowledge and faith, returns the ambiguous in it to the decisive, or, if he is unable, says: "Allah knows best; our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us," and he does not waver. The liar follows the ambiguous and applies it to its apparent sense, and so he anthropomorphises, like the rigid literalists of incarnationism (ahl al-ittihad al-jawamid) who are captivated by mere observation, and he interprets according to his desire in a manner that does not accord with the rules of knowledge nor agree with the decisive, and so he is put to trial.

When it became established by this that He who sent him is the Supreme King, to whom belongs the command (p-464) entirely, that He is doer of what He wills, and that what moves one to benefit from the messengers, peace be upon them, is piety, He consequently said, may He be exalted: ﴿So fear Allah﴾, that is, be in awe of Him because of His majesty, such that you do not proceed with anything except with a clarification from Him, because to Him belongs everything of yours and of others; and it is known to every person of intellect that one does not dispose of another's property in any way except with his permission. ﴿And obey me﴾ in what I convey to you and clarify for you of what keeps you upright, for I take nothing except from Him, and receive nothing except from Him. So my obedience to His command in what pleases Him is the fruit of piety, and the more the pious person increases in acts of obedience, the more his piety increases.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 43, verse 64 (part 1 of 2):

When He commanded them to obey Him, He gave the reason for that by removing the suspicion of what is obeyed in him. He said, emphasizing against their courtesy, which implied denial: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One singled out for majesty and beauty, and so worthy to be feared, ﴿He is﴾, that is, He alone, ﴿my Lord and your Lord﴾. We are equal in servitude through His goodness toward us and His lordship over us. Had He not sent me, He would not have singled me out from you with these clear signs. ﴿So worship Him﴾ by what I command you, because He confirmed me in my command to you to follow what appeared at my hands, so that He became the one who commands, not I.

Since his calling to Allah, peace be upon him, was without any share of worldly gain for himself, that definitively indicated his truthfulness, especially as it was accompanied by miracles, while he himself was in the utmost obscurity, and none of it could be done in any way. He pointed to all of that with his words, by way of inference from what has passed, encouraging it and indicating that it requires obedience: ﴿This﴾, that is, the great matter to which I have called you, ﴿is a path﴾, that is, a very broad, clear road, ﴿straight﴾, with no crookedness in it.

He mentioned what indicates that he brought wisdom from the Injil (the Gospel):

Matthew, one of its four translators, whose translations have become mixed, and most of the narrative is from Matthew, said: When Jesus went out and came to the regions of Tyre and Sidon, behold, a Canaanite woman, and Mark said: a Greek woman, came out from those borders crying out and saying: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David! My daughter is severely possessed by a demon." But he did not answer her with a word. Then his disciples came and asked him, saying: "Send her away, for she cries out after us." He answered and said to them: "I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." Then she came and bowed down to him, saying: "O Lord, help me." He answered: "It is not good to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs." She said: "Yes, Lord, but even the dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters' tables." Then Jesus answered and said to her: "O woman, great is your faith. Let it be to you as you desire." And her daughter was healed from that hour.
