Mark said: He said to her: "For this word, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter." So she went to her house and found the child lying on the bed, and the demon had gone out of her.

They brought to him a man who was deaf and mute, and they begged him to lay his hand on him. He took him aside from the crowd, put his fingers in his ears, spat, then touched his tongue, looked up to heaven, sighed, and said: "Ephphatha," which means "be opened." Immediately his ears were opened, and he heard, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke plainly. He charged them not to tell anyone, but they went and published it abroad, and they were astonished beyond measure, saying: "He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak."

Mark said: Then he came to Bethsaida, and they brought him a blind man and asked him to touch him. He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. He spat on his eyes, laid his hands on him, and asked him: "Do you see anything?" He said: "I see men like trees, walking." Then he laid his hands on his eyes again, and he saw clearly and looked at everything plainly.

He said: Then he came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, and he asked his disciples: "Who do people say the Son of Man is?" Some said: "John the Baptist"; others: "Elijah"; others: "Jeremiah," or "one of the prophets." He said to them: "But who do you say I am?" Simon Peter answered, and said: "You are the Christ." Jesus answered and said to him: "Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes. He said: "Whoever wants to come after me, let him deny himself, and whoever wants to save his life will lose it; and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what will a man profit if he gains the whole world and loses his own soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?"

Luke said: Great multitudes went with him, and he turned and said to them: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it, lest, after he has laid the foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, 'This man began to build and was not able to finish'? Or what king, going to make war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while the other is still a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. So likewise, whoever of you does not forsake all that he has cannot be my disciple."

Luke also mentioned that he, peace be upon him, was at a feast, and he told a parable, because they were choosing the best seats. He said to them: "When you are invited by anyone to a wedding, do not sit down in the best place, lest a more honorable man than you be invited by him, and he who invited you and him come and say to you, 'Give this man your place,' and then you begin with shame to take the lowest place. But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may say to you, 'Friend, go up higher'; then you will have glory in the presence of those who sit at the table with you. For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted." He also said to the one who had invited him: "When you give a dinner or a supper, do not invite your friends, your brothers, your relatives, or your rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind. And you will be blessed, for they cannot repay you, but you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just." When one of those who sat at the table heard this, he said to him: "Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God."

Matthew said: The disciples of Jesus came to him and said: "Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?" He called a little child, set him in their midst, and said: "Truly I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. And whoever receives one little child like this in my name receives me." Mark said: "Whoever receives me does not receive me only, but him who sent me." Luke said: "Whoever receives me receives him who sent me; for he who is least among you all will be great." Matthew said: "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and be drowned in the depth of the sea. Woe to the world because of offenses! For offenses must come, but woe to that man through whom the offense comes! If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it from you. It is better for you to enter life crippled or lame than having two hands or two feet to be cast into everlasting fire." Mark said: "and go into hell, where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched." End.

"And if your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than having two eyes to be cast into hell." Mark said: "For everyone will be seasoned with fire, and every sacrifice will be seasoned with salt. Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another." Luke said: Then he said: "For the sake of people who say they are righteous and despise others, here is a parable: two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus within himself: 'God, I thank You that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.' But the tax collector, standing afar off, would not so much as lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying: 'God, be merciful to me a sinner!' I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted." Then children were brought to him that he might touch them, but when the disciples saw them they rebuked them. But Jesus said: "Let the little children come to me, and do not forbid them, for of such is the kingdom of God. Truly I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will by no means enter it." Matthew said: "Take heed that you do not despise one of these little ones, for the Son of Man has come to save that which was lost. What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them goes astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go to seek the one that went astray?" Luke said: "until he finds it. Truly I say to you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine which did not go astray. Likewise, it is not the will of My Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish." Luke said: Then the tax collectors and sinners drew near to hear him, and the Pharisees and scribes complained, saying: "This man receives sinners and eats with them." So he spoke this parable to them: "What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that is lost until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!' I say to you that likewise there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine just persons who need no repentance. Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls her friends and neighbors, saying, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin which I had lost!' Likewise, I say to you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents." He said: "A certain man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, 'Father, give me the portion of goods that falls to me.' So he divided his livelihood between them. And not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had, traveled to a far country, and there wasted his possessions with prodigal living. But when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that land, and he began to be in need. He went and joined himself to a citizen of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he would have gladly filled his stomach with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything. But when he came to himself, he said: 'How many of my father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, and I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants."' And he arose and came to his father. But when he was still a great way off, his father saw him, had compassion, ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him. And the son said to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son.' But the father said to his servants, 'Bring out the best robe and put it on him, put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet. And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and be merry, for this my son was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.' And they began to be merry. Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. So he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, 'Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf because he has received him safe and sound.' But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and pleaded with him. So he answered and said to his father, 'Look! These many years I have served you, and I never transgressed your command at any time; and yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might be merry with my friends. But as soon as this son of yours came, who has devoured your livelihood with harlots, you killed the fattened calf for him!' And he said to him, 'Son, you are always with me, and all that I have is yours. It was fitting that we should make merry and be glad, for this your brother was dead and is alive again, and was lost and is found.'

He said: "There was a rich man who wore purple and fine linen and enjoyed luxury and pleasure every day. And there was a poor man named Lazarus (al-Azar), lying at his gate, covered with sores, who longed to be satisfied with the crumbs that fell from that rich man's table. The dogs would come and lick his sores. When that poor man died, the angels carried him to the fortress of Abraham (Ibrahim). That rich man also died and was buried, and he lifted up his eyes in the abyss (al-Hawiyah) while in torment. He saw Abraham from afar, and Lazarus in his fortress, and he called out: 'O father Abraham! Have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water to cool my tongue, for I am tormented in these flames.' Abraham said to him: 'My son, remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise received evil things. Now he is comforted here, and you are tormented. Besides all this, between us and you there is a great chasm, far off, so that no one can cross from here to you, nor from there to us.' (p-474) He said: 'I ask you, O father, to send him to my father's house, for I have five brothers, so that he may warn them lest they come to this place of torment.' Abraham said to him: 'They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them.' He said: 'No, O father Abraham! But if someone from the dead goes to them, they will repent.' He said to him: 'If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced even if one rises from the dead.'

And he said to his disciples: 'Stumbling-blocks will surely come, but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him to have a millstone turned by a donkey hung around his neck and be thrown into the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble.' And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 65:

When the clear, ancient path was something that required people to gather upon it and to be in accord while following it, he explained that they (the people of the Book) had, by this admonition, caused something other than what befits them, by His saying: ﴿So the factions differed﴾. He explained that they had multiplied the disagreement by His saying: ﴿the factions﴾, meaning that they were not merely two sects, but many sects. Since it is customary for disagreement to arise between two nations, two tribes, and the like, and since disagreement within a single sect is a marvel, he explained that they were from among the people of the division, so he said: ﴿from among them﴾, meaning a disagreement that arose and began from among the Children of Israel, whom We had made an example for them (p-475), and to whom he said: "I have certainly come to you with wisdom." So from their disagreement he derived His saying: ﴿Woe﴾. It would have been expected to say "for them," but He mentioned the attribute that necessitates woe, for generality and to attach the ruling to it. Since it was in the context of wisdom, which is placing a thing in its most perfect place, the attribute was made to be the wrongdoing to which the disagreement led, so He said: ﴿to those who did wrong﴾, meaning they placed a thing in other than its place, opposing what the Prophet (ﷺ) had brought them of wisdom: ﴿from the punishment of a painful day﴾, meaning a painful one. And if the day is painful, then what is supposed of its punishment?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 66:

When He had made the threat of that Day general to the wrongdoers, so that Quraysh and others entered into it, He followed it with what serves as a reason, presenting it in the form of a question because it is more terrifying. So He said: ﴿Do they await⁠﻿ anything⁠﻿ but⁠﻿ the Hour⁠﻿﻿?⁠﻿ Hmm, the verb has been left bare (without an object-pronoun or particle) to indicate the intensity of its nearness, as if it were before their eyes, so He said: ﴿do they await﴾, i.e., they wait for, ﴿but the Hour﴾, i.e., the Hour of general death, the Resurrection and the standing up, for that is because its matter is certain, as if it were present and being looked at.

When He had placed the Hour first for the sake of awe, as a warning that because its signs are so clearly manifest it is as though it were seen with the eye, shaking them to turn their gaze to seek to see it, He substituted for it, for added awe, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that it come upon them﴿, and He confirmed the possibility of seeing it with His saying: ﴿suddenly﴾. And since the Resurrection may be applied to what is unknown in some respects, He removed this possibility with His saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, i.e., there does not occur to them, at the very time it comes, any kind of knowledge, nor even anything like a hair's breadth of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 67:

When the Hour (al-sa'ah) is applied both to the confinement by death and to the resurrection (al-nashr) by life, he explained what will occur in the second of these, which is the matter they deny, concerning the states of those who are raised, in the form of a new discourse (isti'naf), in answer to one who says: "Will they rise up in the state they are in now?" So He said: ﴿The intimate friends﴾, that is, in the Abode, ﴿on that day﴾, that is, when the Hour occurs, which is the Hour of resurrection (ba'th), which is part of the meaning of the Hour, ﴿will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾. Since it has not become clear to them that their being given respite in life is the cause of their punishment, the follower will say to the one he followed: "You deceived me and so you harmed me," and the one who was followed will say: "Rather, you magnified me and so you diminished me, and you raised me up and so you brought me low," and similar speech that is far more painful. ﴿Except the righteous﴾, those whose affair was preceded by a command to taqwa (God-consciousness) and an exhortation to it.

Since this has shown that there is no enmity between them, but rather that they will be in mutual affection far beyond what they had in the world, because of the affection and mutual support that became evident to them there, it led them to the lasting success of God's good pleasure. He then connected to it a state in which He explained what they will be met with of affection from Him, glorified is He, as an honouring of them and a calming of what that station requires of the terrors: ﴿O My servants﴾, meaning, said to them: this. He singled them out by attributing them to Himself, just as they singled Him out with worship. ﴿No fear shall be upon you today﴾, meaning in no way whatsoever, ﴿nor shall you grieve﴾, meaning: no grief will renew for you over anything that has passed at any of the coming times, because nothing will escape you that would cause you to be sad.

When He addressed them with that which all the people of the standing-place hope for, since every group says, "We are His servants," He singled out those who were intended by it with that which despairs others. And so that the description of piety would not become a source of grief for those among the disbelievers who heard it that Day, and who were unable to attain it, He described the God-fearing (al-Muttaqun) with that which makes attaining their rank easy for others. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Those who believed﴾, meaning they brought this reality into being, ﴿in Our signs﴾, whose greatness is apparent in itself first, and in their being attributed to Us second. ﴿And they were﴾, meaning constantly, with that which belongs to them as a natural disposition and creation, ﴿Muslims﴾, meaning submissive to the commands and prohibitions in the fullest submission. By this they reach the true and complete reality of piety (taqwa).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 70:

When He had mentioned what they would receive as good news and as encouragement for others to join them, in a general manner, He explained that by His saying: ﴿Enter the Garden﴾. And since the abode is not complete except with a pleasant companion, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You and your spouses﴾, meaning your wives who were alike to you in attributes. As for their male companions, they are included in His saying ﴿who were Muslims﴾ [al-Hijr: 2]. ﴿You will be made joyful﴾, meaning you will be honoured and adorned, so you will be delighted with a joy whose effect appears upon you, continuous and renewing forever.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 71:

When this matter was one that drives people toward their state and precedes, for whoever was holding back from their union, al-Biqa'i turned to what the preoccupation with amusement or wealth might be holding him back from, stirring him toward what he was ignorant of and alerting him to what he had neglected. So he said, returning to the third person (al-ghayba) to encourage piety: ﴿They will be served﴾, that is, the God-fearing (al-muttaqin), whom We have made kings by this call, ﴿with platters﴾ (sihaf), the plural of ṣaḥfah, which is a large dish, ﴿of gold﴾, containing in them of the various kinds of food, fruits and sweets that do not enter under imagination.

Since the vessels for drinking in this world are fewer than the vessels for eating, he proceeded according to that familiar pattern, and expressed it with the plural of paucity (jam' al-qilla) in his saying: ﴿and cups﴾ (akwab), the plural of kūb, which is a round, cylindrical-mouthed jug with no handle, from which the hand or the lip may be wide of some part of it, or from which an ugliness would result in some part of the rim of the jug. This signals that there is no need at all to hang anything on it, so that its attributes are not marred by harm (ādhā) or the like.

When he made them desire these unseen things, he summarized with what no sensible person can restrain himself from, in hastening to enter into what pertains to them, and so he said: ﴿And therein﴾, that is, in Paradise. Since pleasure is confined to what is desired, the Exalted said: ﴿whatever the souls desire﴾ of things perceived by the intellect, heard, touched and otherwise, as a reward for them for what they denied their souls of desires in this world. Since what pertains to the things seen is greater than that, He singled it out and said: ﴿and the eyes delight﴾ in the seen things, the highest of which is looking at His noble Face, Exalted is He, as a reward for what they endured of the hardships of longing.

Since that delight is not perfected except with permanence, He said, returning to address (al-khiṭāb), because it is the most noble and sweetest bearer of good news to all who turn to the Book, and turning toward them to encourage them to this reward, as glad tidings to this noble Prophet, upon him be the most excellent prayers and peace, for what he presented at the beginning of the surah and throughout it, of his people reaching the utmost of intellect and knowledge and arriving at the best deed that brings about happiness: ﴿And you therein will abide forever﴾, because of its permanence and the permanence of everything in it, so there is no burden upon you at all, neither fear of cessation nor grief over loss.

Since the preceding clause implied "the Garden for the like of which those who work should work," he joined to it his saying, pointing to its grandeur with the demonstrative of distance: ﴿And that is the Garden﴾, i.e., the one of lofty station, ﴿which﴾. Since inheritance is more suitable for ownership, and since the aspiration of souls is toward acquiring a thing absolutely without distance, he built the verb for the passive object: his saying, may He be exalted, ﴿you have been made to inherit it﴾ (p-480). Since what a person attains through his own striving is more delightful to his soul, owing to his joy in enjoying it and in the deed that was its cause, He said, ﴿because of what﴾, and made clear that the deed was for them like the innate disposition upon which they were created; so the favour truly belongs to their Lord, who purified their souls for them, by His saying: ﴿you used to do﴾, i.e., persevering in that without slackening.

When eating is the most general of needs and the most general of desires, the Exalted said, explaining that all of their eating is for enjoyment (tafakkuh), with nothing in it for sustenance (taqawwut), because there is no depletion in it, neither for strength nor for anything else, so that it would need to be preserved by eating, and so that it would not weaken them: ﴿For you therein is fruit﴾, meaning whatever is eaten for enjoyment, even if it is meat or bread. Since what one enjoys in this world is little, He said: ﴿abundant﴾, and along with the abundance He indicated the continuity of the blessing by the intention of enjoyment with everything in it, through His saying: ﴿of which you eat﴾, meaning not of other than it, from what is eaten for sustenance. ﴿of which you eat﴾ so it never runs out and is not diminished by the eating of those who eat, because it is like flowing water: nothing is taken from it except that its place is filled again by the same amount or more, immediately.

When he had mentioned what is due to the second category, namely the close friends (al-akhilla'), who are the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), as an encouragement for them in piety, he followed it with what is due to their opposites, the people of the first category, as a warning against the likes of their deeds. So he said, as a resumptive and emphatic statement in response to their denial: ﴿Indeed, the criminals﴾, i.e., those firmly established in severing what God commanded be joined, ﴿will be in the torment of Hell﴾, i.e., the Fire, whose nature is to meet those who enter it with scowling, aversion and frowning, just as they used to act when they severed ties with the friends of God, the Exalted, ﴿abiding eternally﴾, because their criminality was a disposition (tab') for them from which they do not separate at all, for as long as they remain.

When He explained His encompassing them like a container encompassing what is in it, and it is known that the Fire does not abate for anyone within it except through something that abates it, such as pouring water on it, reducing its fuel, or some other thing contrary to custom, He made clear that no decrease at all befalls it, as is customary in the torment of this world, because they themselves are its fuel. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning it is aimed at weakening it by some kind of weakness. Thus the negation of taftir (abatement) is a negation of futur (lessening) without the converse. Al-Baydawi said: It is from "fatarat ʿanhu al-humma" (the fever subsided from him) when it abated, and the root is for weakness.

Since awaiting relief is something that lightens the distress of one who is straitened, He negated it with His words: (p-482) ﴿and they in it will be despairing﴾, meaning silent, the silence of despair of deliverance and relief.

Since it may occur to one who lacks insight that this punishment is greater and more than what they deserve, He (glory be to Him) answered with His words, so that their punishment would be increased by their turning to blame themselves and falling into the regret of remorse: ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ in any kind of wrong, because wronging is impossible for Him, exalted is He; ﴿but they themselves were the wrongdoers﴾ by disposition, nature, action and constant practice, ﴿they﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, because they opposed the Bestower of great favours upon them and intended that they would not cease from that as long as they lived. Actions are by intentions, and had they been able not to die, they would not have died.

And since silence is implied by being struck dumb (al-ibsal), He informed that their silence is not constant, because when a person settles himself into one state, the pain may sometimes ease after it. He said, clarifying that they are at such a great distance that they do not hope to address the King, and that although they know they have no hope, they hang their hopes on deliverance, as happens to those who wish for impossible things in this world, so that this would add to their distress: ﴿And they will call out﴾. Then He explained that the one calling out is the keeper of the Fire, so He said, emphasizing the distance with its particle: ﴿O Malik﴾. The reading "yā māl" (يا مالِ) is to indicate that the punishment had weakened them from completing their speech. For this reason they said: ﴿Let your Lord decree an end for us﴾, meaning: ask him a definite request, that the decree is for a death with no equal, and it is death, upon each one of us, and out of their habit of stupidity and coarseness they said: ﴿your Lord﴾, meaning the one who does good to you, and they did not see that God had any favour upon them while they were in that state. There is no doubt that His goodness had not ceased from any existing thing at all, and at the least of that, He does not punish any of them beyond what they deserve. For this reason He made the Fire into levels (darakat) just as the Garden was made into degrees (darajat). It is possible that their saying this was to enrage Him, by what they saw of the Fire's effect upon Him. Their calling out does not contradict their being struck dumb, because it is silence born of despair, so their silence, bound to despair, is constant; therefore they asked for death. The summary is that they do not utter anything indicating hope of relief, but rather they are silent about that forever.

. . Despair, not based on hope of relief through attaining the rank of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun).

When He mentioned their calling out, He resumed mention of their answer with His saying: ﴿He will say﴾, meaning Malik, upon him be peace, emphasizing it to cut off their hopes, because their words here are such that they imply hope, and imply that the mercy of God Most High, which is the object of hope, is specifically for others than them: ﴿Indeed you will remain [in it]﴾.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 78:

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the Hour in connection with ʿĪsā (upon him be peace), saying ﴿And indeed, it is a sign (ʿilm) of the Hour﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 61], and confirmed its matter and explained some of its conditions, until He concluded with what indicates the dissolving of their resolve and the softening of their bridles, while they were not acknowledging this, He said, emphasizing, as an answer to one who sees with partial sight and says: "Is this true?" and expects the answer: ﴿Indeed, We have brought you﴾, that is, in this surah in particular, and the whole Qur'an in general. He called the coming of the messengers a "coming to them" because of the greatness that comes with their coming, which the plural "We" points to, ﴿with the truth﴾, the complete in truthfulness. And since the manifestation of its truthfulness is such that it is not hidden from anyone, but the intensity of hatred and the intensity of love make things appear other than they are, He said, indicating this: ﴿But most of you﴾, that is, O you who are addressed, ﴿are averse to the truth﴾, because of what it contains of restraint from desires; therefore you say that it is not true merely because of your aversion, not because there is some kind of obscurity in its truthfulness.

When this was a report with no possible reply, because the signs were manifest and the majesty of the matter was supreme, the only remaining response was to return. Whoever does not return is only seeking to wage war against the Greatest God. He said, turning away from direct address and placing them in the third person as if they were distant and not worth turning to, balancing it with what is implied: "Return to the manifest truth that has become clear to them." ﴿Or have they resolved a matter?﴾ That is, have they decided ﴿a matter﴾ to reject Our command and oppose Our friends, while knowing that We are watching them.

Since He, glory be to Him, is aware of the hidden intention of their affair and the unseen of their secret, He then made the following consequence of what He had asked about their resolving: it indicates that He knows it, and that He had already settled before its occurrence whatever would remove it, annihilate it and reverse it. This is by way of emphasis against their supposition that they could prevail. So He said: ﴿Then indeed We are the ones who resolve﴾, that is, constantly, over affairs, because of Our knowledge of them before they occur, and Our power and Our will. That is Our attribute, which is not altered in any way: knowledge, power and will. Nothing new has come into being for Us that did not exist before.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 80:

When their persistence was between resolving to confront the All-Powerful openly with enmity, and dealing with Him while He is All-Knowing of concealment and deceit in enmity and open confrontation, and of peace-making and denial, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear﴾ — with the greatness that We possess, which requires all the attributes of perfection — ﴿their secret⁠﴾ and since the intention was to establish that His knowledge, exalted is He, encompasses the hidden and the manifest, with the relation of each of the two to Him being equal, He mentioned them both, (p-486) and placed first that which is by its nature concealed, namely the scheming alluded to by "the making firm" (al-ibram), because the context concerns it. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿their secret⁠﴾, that is, their hidden speech, even if it is in their inner thoughts concerning what disobeys Us. And since it might occur to minds that the intended meaning of "hearing" is only knowledge, because "secret" is what is hidden, and this encompasses what is in the inner thoughts, which are among the things known, He confirmed that the intended meaning is its literal reality by His saying: ﴿and their private conversation⁠﴾, that is, their speech that is raised, as if it were upon a высоко place (najwa), meaning a high spot. Thus it was known that the intended meaning is the literal reality of hearing, and that He, exalted is He, hears everything that can be heard, even if it is not within our power to hear it. We would thus be like the deaf in relation to what we hear of the loud speech, which He does not hear because the power of hearing is absent in Him, not because it is among the things that by right should not be heard.

And since denying the absence of hearing means hearing, He stated it explicitly, saying: ﴿Yes⁠﴾, that is, We hear both kinds equally. ﴿And Our messengers⁠﴾, who are the guarding angels, with the greatness they possess by their relation to Us. And since the presence of the angels with us and their writing down of all our deeds, in a manner that we do not perceive in any way, is a matter of the utmost strangeness, He spoke using "ladā" (with them), which is the expression used to indicate extreme strangeness, saying: ﴿with them they write⁠﴾, that is, they renew the writing whenever there arises what calls for it (p-487), because writing is more effective as a warning, since whoever knows that his deeds are counted and recorded avoids what he fears the consequence of.

After the earlier part of the surah rebuked them and marvelled at their claim that Allah has a son from among the angels, and after He threatened them with His words, ﴿Their testimony will be recorded and they will be questioned﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19], and mentioned their statement, ﴿Had the All-Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20], and their ignorance in it, with His words, ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20], and denied that they had any auditory proof (dalil sam'i) for it, with His words, rebuking them, ﴿Or have We given them a Book?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21], and it passed over the matter of their confusion regarding this and other things, mixing together what had been said earlier with what completed the denial of the auditory proof, by way of the scattered arrangement (al-nashr al-mushawwash, a rhetorical device in which the elements are not presented in their original order), with His words, exalted is He, ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 45], and He arranged in it what His Messenger brought to the People of the Book that confirms what Our Book brought of monotheism (tawhid), and what He threatened against those who turn away from it, until He informed that it is the truth, which has no end at all for any part of it, and that His messengers, glory be to Him, record all their deeds, including their testimony about the angels and others, He returned to speech refuting their objection (shubha) that their worship of them, had it been forbidden, would not have been willed by the One whose mercy is all-encompassing, because the all-encompassing nature of His mercy, in their view, prevents the willing of what is forbidden. So He said, after having denied that they had any auditory proof from any of His messengers, peace be upon them, the words of Allah's: ﴿Say: If the All-Merciful had a son﴾, meaning, the one whose mercy is general, ﴿a son﴾ as you claim. By it is meant the category (jins), because of their claim concerning the angels and others concerning others. The reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, with a damma then a sukun, indicates that it is plural, intending multiplicity.

Since the meaning was: "I did not worship that son, nor do I worship him; had the All-Merciful willed, I would not have abandoned His worship, but He willed my abandoning of it and willed your doing of it," one of the two is certainly a willing of falsehood; otherwise the two contradictories would be combined, in that a thing would be true and false at the same time in one respect, and this is self-evidently impossible. Thus your objection is refuted by a decisive proof. This is how the original argument would have been, but He turned away from it to what conveys its meaning with an addition: that He worships Allah sincerely and does not worship anything else, that one does not deserve the name of worship except what is sincerely devoted to Him. So He said: ﴿Then I am﴾, that is, in rank, ﴿the first of the worshippers﴾ of the All-Merciful, worship in its true sense, which nothing else deserves to be called worship, and which is sincere devotion. That is, I do not worship anything other than Him, neither a son nor anything else, and the All-Merciful did not will for me to worship the son. Or the meaning is: I am the first of the worshippers of the All-Merciful in sincerity, I have never associated anything with Him at any time, of what you have named a son, or a partner, or anything else, and had He willed, I would not have worshipped Him in sincerity. There is no doubt, in your view and in the view of others, that whoever devotes himself sincerely to someone is more deserving of his mercy than others. So if sincerity toward Him were forbidden, He would not have willed it for me, and had the worship of other than Him not been forbidden, He would have willed it for me. And had He a son, He would have willed for me to worship him, for the all-encompassing nature of His mercy toward all His creatures, because they are His creation, and its specific application to me, because I am His servant sincerely devoted to Him, prevents, in your view, that He should make me wretched while I am sincere toward Him. Thus your objection is refuted by a similar argument, indeed a stronger one. This is among the things that hang upon something whose opposite is more fitting for it.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the "an" (in the verse) is negative, meaning: "it is not fitting for Him," that is, "He did not have a son. I am the first to worship Him in rank, and I did not know that He had a son. Had He had a son, I would have known him and worshipped him, seeking nearness to Him through worshipping His son."

When the objection was refuted on one assumption by proof, and on another by an objection stronger than it, and the matter became clear and the truth became evident, namely that He, glory be to Him, wills for one person to do a certain act and for another not to do that act and instead to do its opposite or its contradictory, and it is known with certainty that the two contradictories or the two opposites cannot both be done at the same time, in the same respect, in truth, then it became known from this that the criterion for what is lawful (halal) and unlawful (haram) is His command and prohibition, not His will. And that, were it not so, it would not be known that He is an agent by choice, who specifies whom He wills of His servants with what He wills, after having generalized to them with what He willed. This was the place for declaring Him free of what they attributed (p-490) to Him of falsehood. So He said, declaring Him free of it in a manner that shows that it is not valid to attribute a son to Him at all: ﴿Glory be to the Lord﴾, that is, the Originator and Owner, ﴿of the heavens﴾. Since the context called for declaring Him free of imperfection, the aspect of exaltedness (al-'ulawiyya) was more fitting, because it is further from deficiency and from contradiction. The situation did not require repeating the word "Lord," unlike what comes at the end of al-Jathiya, for that is to establish perfection and to regard all things on an equal footing. So He said: ﴿and the earth﴾, that is, the two of them, in which everything and everyone is subjugated, governed, and in need, and it is not valid that there be for Him, glory be to Him, any relation to it except that of servanthood through origination and nurturing.

Since the distinctive quality of ownership is that one has what no other can reach in any way at all, He said, establishing His ownership of all that is other than Himself, and of what is from other than Himself, and His possession of it, and not repeating the conjunction because the Throne is among the heavens: ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, that is, the one specially associated with it, because it is the distinctive ownership, the Kursi of which encompassed the heavens and the earth, ﴿above what they describe﴾, of His having a son or a partner.

When the truth became clear, the signs of truthfulness shone forth in all that exists, after their doubt had been refuted and their confusion made plain. He knew that they were acting, by placing things in other than their proper places, like one who plunges in and plays. So He said, as a consequence of that: ﴿So leave them﴾ (p-491), meaning: leave them in their worst condition, ﴿to plunge﴾, meaning to act like one who wades into water, placing his foot, which is his support, in something he does not know, and which he may not approve of because he has no knowledge of it. ﴿And play﴾, meaning to act like the player who is absorbed in doing what diminishes him and does not increase him. ﴿Until they meet﴾, meaning that by wasting their lives on what does not benefit them, they act like those who strive to meet ﴿their day which they are promised﴾, a promise with no breach in it, so that their threat will be manifest in it and their warning will be fulfilled.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 84:

When He (glory be to Him) had declared Himself free of having offspring, and indicated this by [stating] that He is the Owner and Sovereign of everything, and since that [attribute] is not necessarily bound to divinity (al-uluhiyyah), He indicated that, along with that, He is the God (al-Ilah), not any other, in both worlds (al-kawnayn), by an self-evident proof whose knowledge all people share. He placed heaven first so that it would be the principle that is followed, because the earth follows it in most matters. So He said, indicating that the relation of all existence to Him is on one equal footing, because He is exempt from need of place or time, linking it to what is implied: a declaration of His transcendence above what they attributed to Him, which is the meaning of ﴿Glory be to Allah﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 82], ﴿and He is the One who is﴾ God (ilah) ﴿in the heaven﴾, that is, the one worshipped, with nothing associated with Him, ﴿and God in the earth﴾, the one toward whom desires are directed in all circumstances, and to whom one sincerely turns at all times of distress (al-idtirar). Thus there is consensus from all who are in the heavens and the earth on His divinity, and His deserving this rank is established, and His exclusive entitlement to it in times of hardship is established, so the remaining times are likewise, without distinction, because He has no partner in such entitlement. Therefore worshipping other than Him is false. In al-Qamus he said: "alaha, i.e., with a fatha, ilahah, uluhah and uluhiyyah: he worshipped with worship. From it comes the word al-Jalalah (Allah), and its origin is ilah, meaning ma'bud (one worshipped), and everything taken as an object of worship is an ilah in the view of the one who takes it. Alaha, like fariha, means: he was bewildered." Thus it is known from this that the prepositional phrase may be attached to ilah.

Since the ilah is not fit for divinity unless He places things in their proper place, such that corruption cannot reach Him and the corruption of a corrupter does not harm them, and this is not possible unless He has perfect knowledge, He said: ﴿And He is the All-Wise﴾, that is, the one of perfect wisdom, which is the knowledge by which judgment is made obligatory, [providing] the establishment of the matter of the one judged in his immediate and ultimate affairs. Since wisdom is knowledge of that for which judgment is made obligatory, He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, that is, the one whose knowledge reaches a degree that does not enter the intellect of the intelligent, [so that] describing Him with it is more emphatic, even if they expanded their thoughts and prolonged their reflection, because ﴿there is nothing like Him﴾ [ash-Shura: 11] in His essence or in any of His attributes, that He might be measured by it. Whoever claims that He has a partner, the one who associates such a partner cannot claim for it what He is described with: the consensus on His divinity and the perfection of His knowledge and wisdom. Thus the invalidity of partnership is established with certainty, in a manner every person understands. There is then no escape, whoever opposes, whoever he may be. Since it is established that He is the God alone, and that He is exempt from partner, offspring, and every blemish of deficiency, He is such that His threat is not to be feared in vain, so His servants do not indulge in vain talk or play. Whoever among them does indulge or play, let him blame none but himself, for his deed is preserved by His knowledge, and so He will recompense him for it by His wisdom.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 43, verse 85:

When He (Exalted be He) declared His Most Holy Essence free from imperfection, and established for Himself the right to divinity by the consensus of His creation, which He had implanted in their natural disposition (fitra) and guided them to through their intellects, He followed that with other proofs by affirming every perfection that the intellects can grasp and that they cannot grasp, explicitly mentioning sovereignty. So He said: ﴿Blessed be He﴾, that is, He is established in a stability that no other stability resembles, because there is no cessation together with blessing (tayammun) and barakah and every perfection. Therefore there is no likeness to Him, so that it could be claimed that He has a son or a partner. (p-494) Then He described Himself with what makes clear His blessedness and His exclusive possession of divinity, so He said: ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾, that is, all of them, ﴿and the earth﴾, likewise, ﴿and what is between them﴾, and between every two of them. The proof of this is the consensus, established upon His unity, at the time of necessity (al-idtirar).

Since His exclusive possession of sovereignty was established, and since a sovereign can only be one who knows his own dominion, and since a claimant may claim and a stubborn opponent may deny regarding sovereignty or knowledge, He cut off these hopes by His saying: ﴿And with Him﴾, that is, with Him alone, ﴿is the knowledge of the Hour﴾, driving it in the manner of what is known to exist, with no room for dispute concerning it. This is a reference to the decisive proofs that are implanted in the primordial fitra, so how much more so for what reason leads to, from the reminder that revelation (al-sam') has alerted us to. And because whoever's exclusive possession of sovereignty is established, it is obligatory to accept his reports, for their own sake, out of fear of his punishments, and out of hope for his blessings. ﴿And to Him﴾, that is, to Him alone and not to another, after the establishment of the Hour, ﴿you will be returned﴾ with the easiest of matters, confirming His sovereignty and cutting off dispute over His oneness. The recitation of the majority, namely all except Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Warsh from Ya'qub, with the second person (bil-khitab), is more intensely threatening than the recitation of the rest with the third person (bil-ghayb), and more indicative of the extreme of anger toward whoever does not turn back to Him in repentance, after removing everything that could cause doubt to arise from it.

(p-495) When the context had directed, with certainty, toward the sense of the omitted phrase, "there is no partner for Him in any of that, nor any offspring, and none of them is able to hold back from returning to Him, just as no one is able to repel His decree and His destiny," He followed it with His saying: ﴿And those they call upon\﻿﻿ — that is, in no way and at no time will they possess (the power of) — ﴾ ﴿other than Him﴾ — that is, they make them objects of calling upon through worshipping them. He indicated their lowliness of rank with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿other than Him﴾, meaning of the lowest rank among the ranks of Him, namely the idols, the angels, humans and others, ﴿intercession﴾ — that is, there will be no intercessor from among them, as they claimed that they were their intercessors. ﴿except he who bears witness﴾ — that is, from among them — ﴿to the truth﴾, that is, the Oneness (of God), which corresponds to reality when it is revealed in the fullest revelation. Likewise, whatever follows from it, for such a one is qualified to intercede, like the angels and the Messiah, peace be upon them. The meaning is that their idols, which they claimed would intercede for them, will not intercede; but He, exalted is He, phrased it in the most eloquent way, because it is like a claim.

Since this was fixed even in the innate natures of the disbelievers, they do not turn to anyone but God at times of hardship; yet they do not remain long before they engage in polytheism that contradicts this. It is as though they had no knowledge, so He said: ﴿while they﴾ — or the state being that — ﴿know﴾ (those who bear witness) — that is, with insight into what they bore witness to. Therefore they do not act contrary to what they witnessed, except out of ignorance of the realization of the meaning of Oneness; hence they suppose they have not departed from it even when they associate others with God. Or the meaning is: they are among the people of knowledge, while the idols are not so. He first used the singular, as an indication that Oneness is an individual obligation (fard ʿayn) upon every person in particular, even if everyone else opposes it; and He used the plural second, as a notice of enjoining good, so that all may unite upon knowledge. Oneness (tawhid) is the foundation upon which no worship is valid without it, and realizing it is the knowledge which no other knowledge equals. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': "All the sects went astray only because they did not understand the meaning of the One in the manner it ought to be understood, for the One may be the origin of number, may be mingled with number, or may be inseparable from number, whereas God, exalted is He, is far above these kinds of unity — end of quote."

So in the verse there is a rebuke to them, in that they affirm Oneness at some times, but when He delivers them, the One whom they affirmed, they make their thanks to Him in ease to be their associating others with Him. It also denies them the claim to this rank, which is the bearing of witness to the truth, because by their association they have stripped themselves of knowledge; and it denies that the angels intercede for them, because that would lead to their having acted contrary to what they know, and that would entail being stripped (p-497) of the knowledge that qualifies one for intercession. Ibn al-Jawzi said: "In the verse is evidence that the condition for all testimonies is that the witness be knowing of what he testifies to."

Since the purpose was to establish the existence of His divinity on earth through the gathering, [the sense is]: "If you were to ask them who rescues them at the time of their distress, they would surely say, 'Allah,' and there is no action for those whom they invoke besides Him in that situation." So He said, linking it to what precedes: ﴿And if you asked them﴾, meaning the disbelievers, ﴿who created them﴾, meaning both the worshippers and the worshipped together, they answered with what indicates the true blindness of the heart, which is innate in them and stamped with the seal of divine wisdom, and they did not stand by the truth in answering such a question when you asked them, ﴿they will surely say, "Allah"﴾, the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection, is the One who created all, and those whom they invoke have no share in that whatsoever. For this reason He based on it His saying: ﴿How then are they turned away?﴾, meaning how, and from what direction, after they have affirmed that He alone holds creation and command, ﴿are they turned away﴾, meaning they turn things from their faces to their backs, whatever the mold, whoever they may be, so they claim that He has a partner, sometimes by way of offspring and sometimes by other means, despite what He has fixed in their natures, by which it is established that He has no partner, because creation and command belong entirely to Him.

(p-498) When He, glory be to Him, had refuted their doubt and thoroughly exposed the futility of their polytheism and their claim of having offspring, and of the other things contained in their false statements attributed to them in this surah, and had established the proofs of truth, set up the demonstrations of sincerity, affirmed what would benefit them and warned them of what would harm them, He concluded all this, swearing with the greatness of His station and the magnitude of His matter, by saying: ﴿Indeed, We have brought you the truth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 78]. Then He confined their affair, in rejecting this, to two divisions and two states: the state of open defiance and the state of covert scheming. He informed that there is no salvation for them in either of these states. He also informed that His messengers record all of their affairs, despite His being free of need of that, owing to His knowledge of what they write and of other things that they do not perceive. This was a great boast, closely and most intimately linked to the doubt they had raised concerning the claim of offspring, so He confirmed its refutation and established its removal. He concluded with an expression of wonder at their state, in that they abandon the faces of affairs and follow their backs. Among the components of this was their behaviour, like that of one who supposes that Allah, glory be to Him, does not hear their speech, which necessitates their seizure, and the speech of His Messenger, which necessitates His support. He then turned to what had preceded of their denial of His hearing their speech. Since their persistence in denial, their distance and their obstinacy only increased with the passing of time (p-499) except in strength, there fell upon the soul of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grief, tenderness, compassion and kindness towards them, and he began to complain of their affair to his Lord, complaining as one who is distressed, secretly and openly, desiring to ease their affair and to lessen their station. Therefore, to express this meaning was chosen the verbal noun of "qāla" (he said), whose form is shared with the passive past form, as an indication that his complaint in this manner had become as if a necessity for him, over which he had no choice in his saying. So it became as a speech without a speaker, or without intention, because it had become a state among his states. He connected to it the pronoun without any prior mention, as an indication that his inner self had been filled with that compassion for them and mercy towards them. So Almighty Allah said, in coordination with their secret which is implied after ﴿Nay﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 80] in His saying: ﴿Do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk? Nay﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 80]. Or it is conjoined to the position of "al-sā'a" (the Hour), meaning "and He knows his speech," as said by al-Zajjaj. He deviated in this aspect, which is the reading of ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah with the genitive case (jarr), for it is clearly connected to that through its conjunction with the word (p-500) ﴿the Hour﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 85]. It was also read irregularly with the nominative case (raf'), and its reasoning is that the waw is for the circumstantial state, meaning: how are they turned away from following Our messenger, who commands them to single Us out in worship, just as We single Ourselves out in creation, while his speech is such in their complaint? Do they suppose that We will not support him when We have sent him? ﴿And his speech﴾, which has come to be constant in his companionship and inseparable from him, becoming one of his states, indicating the manner of his speech and the brokenness of his soul by what the kasra of the verbal noun and its yā' (which is homogeneous with it) indicate. The expression with his saying: ﴿O my Lord﴾ indicates that, by what the particle "yā" (O) indicates of distance, or its implied estimation, and the Lord, which indicates kindness, tenderness, compassion, management and lordship, and particularity and authority. This is contrary to the customary usage in the supplication of those brought near, for it runs throughout the Qur'an with the omission of the vocative particle.

Since sending to them, while the Sender is capable, requires their belief, he confirmed what had become clear to him of their state with his saying, increasing in lamentation and indicating that the delay of their affair shows that their belief is hoped for: ﴿Indeed, these﴾. He did not attribute them to himself by saying "my people" or similar expressions, nor did he name them by the name of their tribe, because of what had grieved him of their state. He used the particle of alerting (hā') before the noun, contrary to the usual original form, indicating that he sensed in himself distance from them, belittling them and considering them of little worth. ﴿A people﴾ (p-501), that is, strong in falsehood, ﴿who do not believe﴾, that is, this act does not renew itself from them.

This being a statement denoting the utmost extent of striving, there followed from it what gladdens him: their faith and their attaining the lofty ranks, which are the outcome of what was hoped for them at the beginning of the surah. All of that came about through the blessing of him (ﷺ), in a context whose outward meaning is threat and whose inward meaning, relative to his knowledge, is good news with emphasis. So He said: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, pardon those among them who turned away, forgiving them, and do not concern yourself with them beyond conveying the message. ﴿And say﴾, that is, to them: ﴿Peace﴾, that is, my affair now is to leave you, with your safety from me and my safety from you. ﴿But they will come to know﴾ by a promise that admits no failure. Thus its outward meaning is a great threat, and the reading of the Madani readers and of Ibn 'Amir with the second-person address is even more threatening. Its inward meaning, from the expression of pardoning them and saying peace, is good news, because they will become scholars, surpassing the nations in knowledge after surpassing them in intellect, as he indicated at the beginning of the surah. Thus they will rise above the nations in walking the paths of reason. How excellent is his (p-502) other part that embraces the first, and a closing that returns to the opening, which descends! O arranger of the pearls! Where do you go away from this lofty structure, and neglect this precious and costly jewel, and go astray from this gleaming, glittering light? Then He raised it high and brought it down, and made the full moon of meanings exalted and preferred.
